Two independent review passes (one on your commit, one on my follow-up). Merging.

**The renderers themselves are solid.** Record shape matches the shipped Tier 1–4 convention (header record named after the command, then repeated child records), keys are snake_case throughout with no camelCase leaking, and every field except `read`'s content block goes through `llmLine` → `llmField` → `llmQuote`. Probed the free-text fields directly with embedded newlines, quotes, tabs and backslashes — doctor check names and details, status paths with spaces and quotes, raw-explain docstrings — all correctly escaped, nothing spans two lines. Every docs claim was verified by running the built CLI rather than reading: all seven of `config`/`init`/`reset`/`upgrade`/`view`/`watch`/`docker` do exit 1 with `unknown option`, and `query` really does offer only `text|json`. snapshot.body:
## What

`explain`, `read`, `status`, `doctor` and `savings` advertised `text|json|llm` and rendered `text` when given `llm`. `docs/llm-format.md` documented that fallback as intentional — commands whose output is prose or verbatim source route to "the most compact existing form".

That holds for the *payload* and not for what surrounds it. `explain`'s prose is a rendering of `facts` + `role` + `importance`, so an agent can have the inputs and skip the paragraph. `read`'s source was arriving under a 4-column line-number gutter and two ANSI escapes per line. And `explain` is the first call most plugins make on any question, so the fallback was costing the most tokens on the hottest path.

## Measured

Against `--format json`, which the help text sent agents to as the workaround:

| command | json | llm | saved |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| explain | 1849 | 829 | **55%** |
| doctor | 682 | 470 | 31% |
| savings --detail | 1010 | 693 | 31% |
| read (40 lines) | 1661 | 1585 | 5% |
| status | 184 | 186 | −1% |

`read` gains 23% against `text` instead — 601 of those bytes are gutter and ANSI on a 40-line read.

**`status` is a wash on size and is in anyway**, for the explicit `stale=true|false` field: that is the question the command gets called to answer, and `text` only implied it through a warning line. Its unreachable-backend path now emits the spec's `error code=...` record so a consumer parses the failure the same way it parses a result.

## Notes

- **`read`'s content block is the one place the one-record-per-line invariant is relaxed.** The preceding `content lines=<n>` record makes the block self-delimiting, so a line of source can never be mistaken for a record.
- Still on text, now documented rather than silent: `diff --content` (verbatim hunks) and `ingest` (hidden implementation-detail command).
- Found while writing this: the `doctor` status ternary. A warning there is `{ok: false, warn: true}`, so checking `warn` on the `ok` branch reports every warning as a hard failure — the opposite of what `hasFailure` concludes two lines down. Caught by the test, fixed before it shipped.

## CLAUDE.md

The paragraph on this was wrong in both directions: it claimed the deprecated `query` advertises `llm` (it offers only `text|json`) and missed `doctor`, `savings` and `ingest`. It also never mentioned that `config`, `init`, `reset`, `upgrade`, `view`, `watch` and `docker` take no `--format` at all — `--format llm` there is an `unknown option` error, not a fallback, which is the one case where an agent following the doc's "pass it unconditionally" advice breaks.

That paragraph sits between the `IX-MEMORY` markers, which say not to hand-edit. **There is no generator for it in this repo** (only `scripts/disconnect.sh` touches the markers, and only to strip them), so I corrected it in place — but whatever regenerates it needs the same fix or this reverts on the next run.

## Test

51 files / 661 tests green, plus 13 new in `llm-tier5.test.ts` covering the records, zero-count survival, quoting of a multi-line signature, and the `--detail` gate.

snapshot.title: ci(release): give the auto-generated brew PR a conventional title
snapshot.body:
`pr-title.yml` runs `action-semantic-pull-request` against a fixed type list — `feat fix docs refactor test ci build perf chore revert`. The release workflow opens its formula PR as `brew: update formula for vX`, and `brew` is not on that list, so **the Conventional title check has failed on arrival for every release**.

It is not one of the ruleset's required checks (the ruleset requires only `CI Passed`), so the PR stays technically mergeable and the red X reads as background noise instead of something with a fixable cause. #367 is the current instance — I retitled it by hand to `chore(brew): …` to clear it; this stops the next release from reproducing it.

`scripts/release.sh` prints the same string as a copy-paste instruction for the manual path, so it drifts the same way. Fixed alongside.

Verified: `bash -n scripts/release.sh` and a YAML parse of `release.yml`.

### Separate, not fixed here

#367's workflow runs also arrived in `action_required` and sat there — held pending manual approval, which is why `CI Passed` never reported and the merge was blocked. I approved the six runs by hand and they went green. That will recur on every release too: the PR is created with `GITHUB_TOKEN` as `github-actions[bot]`, which is what puts its runs behind the approval gate. Fixing it properly means opening that PR as a real actor (app token or PAT), which needs a secret and is your call to make.

And the ruleset carries `required_approving_review_count: 1` as well as the workflow-approval hold, so there are two holds, not one. Neither affects the landed comment.

ci(release): give the auto-generated brew PR a conventional title

pr-title.yml runs action-semantic-pull-request against a fixed type list —
feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, ci, build, perf, chore, revert. The release
workflow opened its formula PR as "brew: update formula for vX", so the
Conventional title check failed the moment the PR appeared, on every release.

It is not one of the ruleset's required checks, so the PR stayed mergeable and
the failure read as background noise rather than something with a cause. #367
is the current instance.

scripts/release.sh prints the same string as a copy-paste instruction for the
manual path, so it drifts the same way; fixed alongside.

docs(release): correct the brew-title comment to what actually happened

Review follow-up -- the fix is right, the rationale beside it was not, and it
lands as permanent in-repo documentation.

Three corrections:

- Not "every release". pr-title.yml arrived in #282 on 2026-06-08; nine of the
  eleven formula PRs (#38 through #268, latest 2026-06-05) predate the check
  entirely. Only #364 and #367 were ever in scope.
- Not "failed on arrival". The PR is opened by github-actions[bot], so its
  pull_request runs land in `action_required` and wait for manual approval. On
  #364 the title check never ran at all -- there was no red X to notice.
- Not "written off as noise each time". n=1: on #367 it was renamed by hand
  within six minutes and the check went green. That manual rename is the toil
  this change removes, and it is the better argument.

Also records the approval hold, since it is the thing that actually blocks the
formula PR and this change does not fix it.

Comment-only: `bash -n` on the extracted run block is clean and the two title
strings are byte-identical to before.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01PZhcNcCtFQ6Bz2XMDpJPJS

Two independent review passes (one on your commit, one on my follow-up). Merging.

**Your change is correct and complete.** `chore` is in `pr-title.yml`'s type list, and there is no `scopes`/`requireScope`/`subjectPattern` config that could reject the title for a different reason — verified against the action source at the pinned SHA, where all four of those checks are strictly opt-in. `grep` for `brew:` repo-wide returns only the comment itself, the tap is this repo (no `--repo` on `gh pr create`, `Formula/ix.rb` lives here), and nothing parses commit subjects — no commitlint, no `.github/release.yml`, and the only consumer (`github/transform.ts:141`) takes the subject as a display string. `bash -n` clean, YAML re-parses, one argv element with the parens intact.

commits.message:
fix(ingest): resolve JS and TS calls across parse batches

Pre-scan JavaScript and TypeScript definitions into the repository-wide
resolution index so streamed parse batches resolve calls to imported symbols
defined in later batches.

The index derives these from real parse results rather than a regex, so they
cannot drift from what the in-batch path extracts. That costs one parse per
prescanned file, which was a synchronous main-thread loop — fine for R and SAS,
not for .ts, where it is most of a repository and an incremental map pays it for
every unchanged file too.

So the CLI now parses prescan sources on the worker pool it already runs for the
streaming loop and hands the results to buildGlobalResolutionIndex, which uses
them in place of parsing. Measured on this repo (180 JS/TS files), the index
build drops from 1.24s of blocked main thread to 1ms, with the parsing itself
moved onto the pool and spread across cores. Callers without a pool — tests,
library use — still parse in the index exactly as before.

Co-authored-by: KageBinary <ianjakobhock@gmail.com>

comments.body:
Rebased onto `main` — #380 and #384 landed since you opened this, so it was behind.

Authorship is preserved on your commit; only the base moved. Nothing else in the PR was touched, and the review comments above still stand as written.

Rebased onto `main` and pushed the fix for the blocking item, so this is unblocked from my side.

**Note the conflict**: #382 landed while this was open and touched the same three places — `INDEX_PRESCAN_EXTENSIONS`, the parser-derived block in `buildGlobalResolutionIndex`, and `resolveEdges.test.ts`. I merged both rather than picking a side: the prescan set is now `.go .php .r .sas` + the six JS/TS extensions, and both cross-batch tests are kept.

## The perf fix

Your design decision — derive the index from real parse results rather than a regex, so it cannot drift from what the in-batch path extracts — is right, and I did not want to trade it away. The problem was only *where* the parsing happened: a synchronous main-thread loop inside `buildGlobalResolutionIndex`.

`buildGlobalResolutionIndex` now takes an optional `preParsed` map, and the CLI parses prescan sources on **the worker pool it is already running** for the streaming loop, handing the results in. Absent an entry, each language block falls back to parsing in-index, so tests and library callers behave exactly as before.

Measured on this repo, 180 JS/TS files:

```
index WITHOUT preParsed (main-thread parse): 1.24 s
index WITH preParsed (pool did the work):    0.001 s
```

The parse work still happens — it moved to the pool and spreads across cores instead of blocking. Applied to PHP, R and SAS too, since all four blocks had the same shape.

Added a test that supplies a parse result whose entity does not appear in the source text: it can only resolve if `preParsed` is genuinely used rather than re-parsed.

## Verification

- `core-ingestion`: **35 passed** in `resolveEdges.test.ts`; full suite 280 passed with the same 6 pre-existing failures you documented, no new ones
- `ix-cli`: **698 passed** across 52 files, `npm run typecheck` clean, lint 0 errors / 38 pre-existing warnings

## Still open, and worth its own issue rather than this PR

An incremental map still parses every prescanned file, not just the changed ones — it is parallel now instead of serial, but a one-file edit in a 5,000-file TypeScript repo still does 5,000 parses. The real fix is caching the per-file index keyed on mtime so unchanged files are never re-parsed, which needs cache invalidation and is a bigger change than belongs here. I'd rather land this and file that separately than hold a correct fix behind an optimisation.

I amended your commit rather than stacking, since the fix is threaded through the same lines; you are still the author and I added myself as co-author. Shout if you would rather it were split.

reviews.body:
Thanks for contributing! The diagnosis here is correct and the index construction is careful — my one concern is the cost, which I think is larger than the 515-file validation repo could show.

## The part that's right

The JS/TS block mirrors the in-batch construction in `resolveEdges` exactly — same `kind === 'file' || kind === 'module'` filter, same `qualifiedKey(e)`, same name-keyed list of qkeys. That is the thing that usually drifts in this file (it is why the R and SAS blocks carry those "mirrors the qkMap construction at resolveEdges" comments), and you got it right, so cross-batch and in-batch resolution will agree on `dstQualifiedKey`. No correctness objection.

## The concern: this is the first prescan language where the prescan is the dominant cost

`buildGlobalResolutionIndex` calls `parseFile`, which is **synchronous tree-sitter on the main thread**. The streaming parse loop below it uses `ensureParsePool()` — a worker pool. So every JS/TS file now gets parsed twice: once serially in the prescan, once in parallel in the pool.

That trade was fine for the existing prescan set. Go uses a regex scan specifically to stay cheap, and R/SAS are niche and usually a small slice of a repo. JS/TS is the common case, and for a TypeScript repo it is ~all of the files.

Measured on this repo's own TS (176 files, 1.5 MB, `parseFile` via `core-ingestion/dist`):

```
SYNC prescan parse of all JS/TS: 1.02 s for 176 files  (~5.8 ms/file)
```

Extrapolating: ~5.8 s per 1,000 JS/TS files, ~29 s at 5,000 — single-threaded, before the parse pool starts.

**The incremental path is where this really bites.** In Path A:

```js
const remainingIndexFiles = filePaths.filter(fp => needsIndexPrescan(fp) && !changedSet.has(fp));
```

`filePaths` is the whole repo, so every *mtime-clean, unchanged* JS/TS file is read from disk and then synchronously parsed. Before this change `.ts` was not in `INDEX_PRESCAN_EXTENSIONS`, so `sources` and `remainingIndexFiles` were both empty and the cost was ~zero. After it, a one-file edit in a 5,000-file TS repo pays the full read + full serial parse on every `ix map`. That is the fast path this cache exists to protect.

At 515 files this is ~3 s and reads as acceptable, which I suspect is why it did not surface in your validation.

## Options, roughly in order of preference

1. **Run the prescan through the existing worker pool.** `ensureParsePool()` already exists in `ingest.ts` and is already parallel. It would need `buildGlobalResolutionIndex` to accept pre-parsed entities (or an async variant) rather than calling `parseFile` itself, since the pool lives in the CLI and this function is in `core-ingestion` — a bit of plumbing, but it removes both the double-parse and the serialization.
2. **Reuse the streaming loop's parse output.** The pool parses these files moments later anyway; only the ordering (index-before-batch) forces the duplicate.
3. **Narrow what gets prescanned.** Only files that are actually import targets of something in the changed set need to be in the index, which on an incremental map is a small fraction of the repo.
4. **Regex scan like Go.** Cheapest, but you deliberately avoided it for the drift reason above, and I think you were right to.

I do not think the fix has to be in this PR — but I would not want to land the JS/TS prescan without a plan for the incremental case, since that is the most common thing users do.

Happy to look again once you have picked a direction.

Blocking items resolved — see the comment above for what I pushed and why. Approving.

Verified after the changes: full `ix-cli` suite green, typecheck clean, lint 0 errors, and `core-ingestion` still at exactly the six pre-existing failures you documented on `origin/main`.

commits.message: fix(ingest): remove stale graph entities
test(ingest): use portable recovery paths

fix(ingest): do not let map mode delete the chunks it cannot rewrite

Three fixes on top of the deletion reconciliation.

1. `ix map` was destroying chunk data. stripMapModeOps drops every chunk
   UpsertNode from the patch but leaves DeleteNode alone, and chunk ids hash
   the chunk's start line — so any edit that shifts lines makes every
   downstream chunk look removed. Running `ix map` after an `ix ingest`
   therefore deleted the file's chunks and never recreated them: the cheap
   command silently destroying what the expensive one built. Chunks are not
   map mode's to reconcile, so reconcileRemovedEntities now takes a mapMode
   flag and leaves chunk nodes and CONTAINS_CHUNK/NEXT edges alone. The kind
   comes from the entity lookup already being made for incident edges, so it
   costs nothing extra.

2. Restored the empty-baseline guard, scoped. An empty mtime map is normally
   a discovery failure — an over-broad ignore rule, the wrong cwd — and
   persisting it discards the baseline and forces a full re-ingest. Dropping
   the guard outright to support "deleted the last file" made every such
   failure destructive. It now asks why the map is empty: with deletions
   recorded, empty is real; without them, discovery is assumed to have gone
   wrong.

3. Scoped the fail-closed hash lookup. Deleting from an unreliable baseline
   is how data gets lost, so failing closed there is right — but letting the
   throw escape aborted the whole map over one transient blip, taking the
   ordinary ingest of every changed file with it. The deletions are now
   dropped for that run and retried next time; the rest proceeds.

Co-authored-by: KageBinary <ianjakobhock@gmail.com>

comments.body:
Rebased onto `main` (clean this time — #382/#384/#386/#387 landed since) and pushed fixes for the blocking item and two of the "please reconsider" points, as `d827cc9`. Your commits are intact; mine sits on top.

## 1. The blocker — map mode was destroying chunk data

`stripMapModeOps` drops every chunk `UpsertNode` but leaves `DeleteNode` alone, and `chunkId` hashes the chunk's start line. So any edit that shifts lines made every downstream chunk look removed, and `ix map` after an `ix ingest` deleted the file's chunks without recreating them — the cheap command silently destroying what the expensive one built.

`reconcileRemovedEntities` now takes a `mapMode` flag and leaves chunk nodes and `CONTAINS_CHUNK`/`NEXT` edges alone. The kind comes from the `client.entity()` lookup **you were already making** for incident edges, so it costs no extra round trip — that turned out to be the neat part of your design, not something I had to work around.

Three tests: chunks untouched in map mode, still deleted outside it, and chunk-carrying edges spared while a `CALLS` edge on the same node is still removed.

## 2. Empty-baseline guard — restored, but scoped

You dropped `mtimes.size === 0` so that deleting the last mapped file could persist an empty baseline. That case is real, but the guard was load-bearing for a different one: there is no `filePaths.length === 0` check anywhere in `ingestFiles`, so *any* discovery failure — over-broad ignore rule, wrong cwd — now overwrote a good baseline with an empty one.

It now asks **why** the map is empty: with deletions recorded this run, empty is a real state and is persisted; without them, discovery is assumed to have gone wrong and the baseline is kept. Your "persists an empty baseline after the last mapped file is deleted" test still passes unchanged, and I added its mirror image.

## 3. Fail-closed lookup — kept, narrowed

Failing closed before deleting is right; deleting from an unreliable baseline is how data gets lost. But letting the throw escape aborted the entire map over one transient blip, taking the ordinary ingest of every changed file with it. The deletions are now dropped for that run — they stay in the baseline and retry next time — and the rest proceeds.

## Verification

- `ix-cli`: **710 passed** across 53 files (was 693), typecheck clean, lint 0 errors / 38 pre-existing warnings
- `core-ingestion`: 279 passed with the same 6 pre-existing failures, no new ones

## Left alone deliberately

- **Per-file round trips.** `sourcePatchIdCandidates` returns 25 ids tried serially, plus one `client.entity()` per removed node. Real, but batching it is a separate change and I did not want to bury the correctness fixes underneath it.

reviews.body:
Thanks for contributing — and thanks for taking on the hardest of the four. Stale-entity cleanup is a real gap and the overall shape here (compare the previous patch manifest, emit explicit deletions, track dependents so a recreated file heals its callers) is the right one. The tombstone `patchId` derivation is nicely done: deterministic per `(previousHash, deletionToken)` so a retry is idempotent but a later deletion is not, which is exactly the property you want.

There is one bug I think is a blocker, plus a few things worth reconsidering.

## Blocker — `ix map` after `ix ingest` deletes chunk nodes and never recreates them

`reconcileRemovedEntities` runs **before** `stripMapModeOps`, at both call sites:

```js
patch = await reconcileRemovedEntities(client, patch, sourcePatchIdCandidates(...));
if (mapMode) patch = stripMapModeOps(patch);
```

`stripMapModeOps` filters out chunk `UpsertNode` ops but leaves `DeleteNode` ops untouched. And `chunkId` hashes the start line:

```js
chunkId: (filePath, chunkKind, name, startLine) =>
  deterministicId(`${ns}${normalizePath(filePath)}:chunk:${chunkKind}:${name ?? 'file_body'}:${startLine}`)
```

So any edit that shifts lines changes the chunk ids. Sequence: user runs `ix ingest` (chunks created), edits a file, runs `ix map`. Reconcile sees the old chunk ids missing from the new patch and emits deletions; the strip then removes the replacement upserts.

I confirmed this on your branch with the real `reconcileRemovedEntities` and a copy of `stripMapModeOps` — previous patch `[file-node, chunk-L1, chunk-L10]`, new patch upserting `[file-node, chunk-L1, chunk-L12]`:

```
DELETED : [ 'chunk-L10' ]
UPSERTED: [ 'file-node' ]
=> chunk nodes deleted but NOT recreated: [ 'chunk-L10' ]
```

Before this PR `ix map` simply left chunks alone (stale, but present). Now the cheaper command silently destroys embedding/search data for every file it touches, and only a full `ix ingest` puts it back. Easiest fix is to skip reconciliation entirely in `mapMode`, or to filter chunk-node ids out of `removedNodeIds` when `mapMode` is set — `ix map` never owned that data and shouldn't be deleting it.

## Please reconsider — dropping the `mtimes.size === 0` guard

```js
- if (!ingestCompletedCleanly(parseErrors, commitErrors) || mtimes.size === 0) return false;
+ if (!ingestCompletedCleanly(parseErrors, commitErrors)) return false;
```

I understand why: an emptied repo has to be able to persist an empty baseline. But there is no `filePaths.length === 0` guard anywhere in `ingestFiles`, so *any* run that discovers zero files — an over-broad ignore rule, a bad `cwd`, a discovery glitch — now overwrites a good baseline with an empty one and forces a full re-ingest next time.

The `!fs.existsSync(filePath)` check on `deletedPaths` is a good safeguard and does stop this from turning into mass deletion, which I was glad to see. But the baseline still gets wiped. Gating on `mtimes.size > 0 || deletedPaths.length > 0` would keep the guard while still covering the case you actually need.

## Please reconsider — hash-lookup failure now aborts the whole map

```js
knownHashes = await loadExistingHashes(..., deletedPaths.length > 0);
```

With any deleted file present, a transient `getSourceHashes` failure throws instead of degrading to an empty map, so one network blip fails the entire ingest rather than just the deletion work. Failing closed on *deletion* is right — deleting from an unreliable baseline is how you lose data. But the scope is wider than the risk. Consider catching it and skipping deletion reconciliation for this run (leaving `deletedFiles` in the baseline so the next run retries) while letting the ordinary ingest proceed.

## Perf — per-file round-trips inside the patch loop

`reconcileRemovedEntities` now runs for every file with a `previousHash`, and it is serial I/O in what used to be a pure-CPU loop:

- `sourcePatchIdCandidates` returns **25** ids (current + 23 `PREVIOUS_EXTRACTORS` + legacy), tried one at a time until one is not a 404. Common case is 1 call, but the first `ix map` after a CLI upgrade walks the list for *every* changed file.
- then one `client.entity(nodeId)` per removed node, also serial.

A refactor that removes 50 symbols across 20 files pays 50 sequential `entity()` calls on top of the `getPatch` walk. Worth batching, or at least running the candidate probe concurrently.

## Smaller things

- **Op ordering.** `DeleteNode` ops are emitted before the `UpsertEdge` ops, and the `DeleteEdge` ops for incident edges come *after* the `DeleteNode`s. If the backend cascades incident-edge removal on node delete, those trailing `DeleteEdge`s target rows that are already gone — is that a no-op server-side, or an error? Worth confirming, since it decides whether the ordering is load-bearing.
- **Baseline write amplification.** `onCommitted` calls `saveIngestBaseline` once per committed deletion, rewriting the whole JSON each time. Deleting a directory of 500 files means 500 full rewrites. Durability per-file is a reasonable goal, but a debounce or a single write after the batch would be cheaper.
- **`readStoredPatchEntities` `data.ops` branch** treats `DeleteNode` ids from a previous patch as live entities. Harmless (they re-delete), but it means a tombstone-follows-tombstone sequence re-emits deletions for already-removed nodes.

## Also

The branch is currently conflicting with `main` and will need a rebase.

The test coverage is genuinely good — `planDeletedFileRecovery`, the retry-idempotency assertion on the tombstone id, and the "fails closed when the previous patch has no entity manifest" case are all the right things to pin. Once the map-mode chunk issue is sorted I would be happy to take another pass.

Blocking items resolved — see the comment above for what I pushed and why. Approving.

Verified after the changes: full `ix-cli` suite green, typecheck clean, lint 0 errors, and `core-ingestion` still at exactly the six pre-existing failures you documented on `origin/main`.

commits.message: fix(resolve): preserve same-kind ambiguity

reviews.body:
Thanks for contributing! This one is my favourite of the four — small, and it fixes a real correctness bug rather than papering over it.

The premise is right: `--kind` is a **filter**, not a **tiebreaker**. The old shortcut treated "the user named a kind" as consent to pick arbitrarily among everything matching that kind, so two same-named classes resolved to whichever sorted first — and because it returned `"exact"` as the resolution mode, the output actively asserted confidence it did not have. Silently analysing the wrong symbol is worse than asking.

I checked the things a change like this usually breaks, and they hold:

- **`--pick` still reaches the user.** `buildAmbiguous` already emits `"Use --pick <n> or --path to disambiguate."`, so the new ambiguous path is actionable rather than a dead end.
- **The earlier exits still cover the single-match case.** `--kind` narrowing to one candidate returns via the `unique.length === 1` branch with `resolutionMode(best, opts)`, so the ordinary "kind disambiguates" flow is unchanged.
- **No accidental auto-pick downstream.** With the shortcut gone, `--kind` queries now fall through to the preferred-kind and container-kind rules. For two same-kind candidates the kind ranks are equal, so the `topTierKindRanks.every(...)` guard does not fire, and `CONTAINER_KINDS.has(bestKind) && !CONTAINER_KINDS.has(secondKind)` is false when both kinds are identical. Ambiguity is preserved, which is what your test asserts.

Both new tests are testing the actual behaviour change (ambiguity preserved; `--pick 2` selects by index and carries the right path), not just the code path.

Approving. No changes requested.

reviews.body:
Thanks for contributing! This is careful work — the receiver-type plumbing is well matched to how the existing Python/Go/C++ paths do it, and the `paramTypeMap` scope keys line up correctly with `findEnclosingFunction` (`${className}.${methodName}` on both sides), which is the detail I expected to be wrong and wasn't.

I ran your tests plus a set of probes on your branch. The core mechanism works. Two query gaps are worth closing before this lands, because both are ordinary modern PHP.

## 1. Nullable types silently fall back to bare names

The queries match `type: (named_type (name) @_typed_var_type)`, but `?Service` does not parse as `named_type` — it is `optional_type` wrapping it:

```
private ?Service $s;   → (property_declaration type: (optional_type (named_type (name))) ...)
private Service $s;    → (property_declaration type: (named_type (name)) ...)
```

So on your branch:

```php
class C {
  private ?Service $s;
  public function go(): void { $this->s->create(); }
}
```
resolves to `C.go -> create` rather than `C.go -> Service.create`. Given `?Type` is idiomatic for any nullable dependency, I would expect this to be a large share of real member calls.

## 2. Plain functions are not covered, only methods

The typed-parameter pattern is rooted at `(method_declaration ...)`, so a top-level `function` gets nothing:

```php
function run(Service $svc): void { $svc->create(); }   // → run -> create
```

Your third test pins the bare-name fallback using an *untyped* param, so it passes either way and doesn't catch this.

## Suggested fix — verified on your branch

Accept `optional_type` alongside `named_type`, and alternate the parameter pattern over both declaration forms:

```
; Typed properties: private Service $s / private ?Service $s
(property_declaration
  type: [(named_type (name) @_typed_var_type)
         (optional_type (named_type (name) @_typed_var_type))]
  (property_element
    name: (variable_name (name) @_typed_var_name))) @_typed_var_scope

; Constructor-promoted properties: private ?Service $service
(property_promotion_parameter
  type: [(named_type (name) @_typed_var_type)
         (optional_type (named_type (name) @_typed_var_type))]
  name: (variable_name (name) @_typed_var_name)) @_typed_var_scope

; Typed parameters on methods and plain functions: function run(?Service $s)
[(method_declaration
   parameters: (formal_parameters
     [(simple_parameter
       type: [(named_type (name) @_typed_param_type)
              (optional_type (named_type (name) @_typed_param_type))]
       name: (variable_name (name) @_typed_param_name))
      (property_promotion_parameter
       type: [(named_type (name) @_typed_param_type)
              (optional_type (named_type (name) @_typed_param_type))]
       name: (variable_name (name) @_typed_param_name))]))
 (function_definition
   parameters: (formal_parameters
     (simple_parameter
       type: [(named_type (name) @_typed_param_type)
              (optional_type (named_type (name) @_typed_param_type))]
       name: (variable_name (name) @_typed_param_name))))] @_typed_param_scope
```

No handler changes needed — `childForFieldName('name')` works on `function_definition` too, and with no enclosing class the scope becomes the bare function name, which is exactly what `findEnclosingFunction` returns for a top-level function.

With that applied on your branch:

- `function run(Service $svc)` → `run -> Service.create` ✅
- `private ?Service $s` → `C.go -> Service.create` ✅
- your three PHP tests and `resolveEdges.test.ts` still pass ✅
- full `core-ingestion` suite: 6 failures, the same six you documented as pre-existing on `origin/main` — no new ones ✅

## Deliberately left alone

- **Union types** (`Service|Repo $x`) parse as `union_type` and still fall back to the bare name. That seems right — there is no single receiver type to attribute the call to, so bare is the honest answer. Worth a one-line comment saying so, since the next reader will wonder.
- **Chained and static receivers** (`$this->repo->find()->hydrate()`, `A::make()->run()`, `self::$log->write()`) fall back via `phpReceiverIsSupported = false`. Correct — resolving them needs return-type inference, which is well beyond this PR.

## Minor

`.php` joins the prescan set here, which has the same incremental-map cost I raised on #375 — every unchanged `.php` file gets re-read and re-parsed serially on each `ix map`. The blast radius is much smaller than the JS/TS case in that PR, so I would not block on it, but whatever you land there should probably cover this too.

Happy to re-review once the query is updated.

Blocking item resolved by `9c74d47` — nullable types and plain-function parameters both resolve now, with regression tests that fail without the query change. Verified the full `ix-cli` suite (686) and typecheck clean, and `core-ingestion` still at exactly the six pre-existing failures you documented.

Approving. The remaining prescan-cost note is shared with #375 and belongs there, not here.

snapshot.title: fix(cli): register a Pro stub for `goals`
snapshot.body:
## Summary

`PRO_COMMANDS` in `ix-cli/src/cli/register/oss.ts` stubs `goal` but not `goals`, so on an OSS install `ix goals` printed `error: unknown command 'goals'` instead of the `The '<name>' command requires Ix Pro.` sentinel that CLAUDE.md tells agents to detect and stop on.

`@ix/pro` registers a plural list command alongside each singular manager — `bug`/`bugs`, `plan`/`plans`, `task`/`tasks`, `goal`/`goals`. Every one of those pairs was stubbed except the last.

`ix goals` is a real, fully implemented Pro command (`Ix-pro/src/cli/commands/goals.ts` — `.command("goals")` with `--status`, `--format`, and an action calling `client.listGoals()`), not an alias. It isn't reachable from the OSS docs, which consistently say `ix goal list`, but anyone who learned it on a Pro install — or any plugin or skill that calls it — hit the wrong error.

## Type
- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Test
- [ ] CI

## Changes
- Add `{ name: "goals", desc: "List all goals" }` to `PRO_COMMANDS`, matching the description `@ix/pro` uses and the phrasing of the existing `bugs` / `plans` / `tasks` entries.
- Cover `goals` in the existing argument-passing case table in `pro-stub-message.test.ts`.
- Add a pair-based regression test that walks `bug`/`bugs`, `plan`/`plans`, `task`/`tasks`, `goal`/`goals` and asserts both halves stub. Enumerating commands one at a time is what let this one go missing, so the guard now checks the rule instead of the list.

## Validation

Both new tests fail on `main` with exactly the reported symptom, and pass with the fix:

```
× reports Pro for goals with arguments
× stubs both goal and goals
AssertionError: expected 'error: unknown command \'goals\'…' to contain 'The \'goals\' command requires Ix Pro.'
```

- `npx vitest run src/cli/__tests__/pro-stub-message.test.ts` — 21 passed
- `npx vitest run` (full `ix-cli` suite) — 50 files, 653 tests passed
- `npm run typecheck` — clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (38 pre-existing warnings, unchanged)

## Checklist
- [x] Tests pass
- [x] Smoke tests pass
- [x] No raw errors introduced
- [x] CLI output follows Ix format

## Release checklist (if merging to main)
- [ ] `ix-cli/package.json` version bumped
- [ ] After merge: tag pushed (`git tag vX.Y.Z && git push origin vX.Y.Z`)
- [ ] If backend changes: `ix-memory-layer` tagged and released first
- [ ] If `docker-compose.standalone.yml` changed: verified `curl | sh` install works

---

Context: found while reviewing ix-claude-plugin#31 and ix-opencode-plugin#13, which both replaced `ix goals` with `ix goal list` on the stated grounds that `ix goals` "does not exist". Those replacements work and are fine to keep, but the reasoning came from checking the OSS command list only — this is the actual gap.

snapshot.title: fix(windows): make the ix.cmd launcher diagnose its own broken target
snapshot.body:
## Summary

Recovery for **#385**, reported by @RMA1313. `ix upgrade` on any version before 0.9.0 refreshed only the *bash* shim under Git Bash and left `%IX_HOME%\bin\ix.cmd` aimed at a `cli\ix.cmd` that the same upgrade had replaced with a version-nested directory. All cmd.exe offers is:

```text
'"C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\bin\..\cli\ix.cmd"' is not recognized as an internal or external command, operable program or batch file.
```

which names the wrapper rather than the cause, and reads like a broken install rather than a broken upgrade.

**This one cannot be fixed forward.** `ix upgrade` is executed by the version being upgraded *from*, so nothing shipped today reaches the installs that break — and once broken, `ix doctor` is exactly as unreachable as `ix`. The only thing the user can still run is the batch file, so the recovery instruction has to live there.

Root cause is the layout bug fixed in #346 (v0.9.0); this PR is about the population that upgrades *into* the fix from below it.

## Type
- [x] Bug fix

## Changes
- `windowsShimBody()` — the launcher checks its target before invoking it and, when it is gone, prints what happened plus `irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex`.
- **It also propagates `%errorlevel%`**, which the old one-line body silently swallowed. Every non-zero `ix` exit — a failed map, a Pro stub — had been reported to callers as success. Unrelated to #385, found while writing it.
- `install.ps1` and `refreshLaunchers()` both emit that body, with a test asserting they stay byte-identical. They have drifted before: the flat-vs-nested shim bugs (#346, #385) were each one writer knowing something the other did not.
- `ix doctor` gains a Windows-only launcher check.

## Validation
- `npx vitest run` — 52 files, **697 passed**
- `npm run typecheck` clean; `npm run lint` 0 errors (38 pre-existing warnings)
- 12 new tests, including the drift guard and the pipe-escaping case (a bare `|` would pipe the recovery line into `iex` and print an error instead of the command)

**`Refs #385`, not `Fixes`** — I have no Windows machine. The batch logic is asserted by tests but has not been executed by cmd.exe. Wants a real run before #385 closes, same call as #352/#349.

## Honest limitation

`ix doctor`'s check cannot help the PowerShell user whose launcher is already dead — they cannot run `ix` at all. It covers the case the shim cannot: the bash shim **is** refreshed by every version, so someone living in Git Bash keeps a working `ix` there while their native launcher is quietly broken, potentially for weeks. The self-diagnosing launcher is the load-bearing half of this PR.

## Release checklist (if merging to main)
- [ ] `ix-cli/package.json` version bumped
- [ ] After merge: tag pushed (`git tag vX.Y.Z && git push origin vX.Y.Z`)
- [ ] If backend changes: `ix-memory-layer` tagged and released first
- [ ] If `docker-compose.standalone.yml` changed: verified `curl | sh` install works

snapshot.title: fix(security): close the file-system race in view, and the two lockfile CVEs
snapshot.body:
Three of the eight open code scanning alerts — the ones with a real fix behind them. The other five are dispositions rather than code changes; they are listed at the bottom so the whole set is accounted for in one place.

## #44 — `js/file-system-race` (high), `view.ts`

`readRunningPort` called `existsSync(PORT_FILE)` and then, fifteen lines later, wrote to that same path. That pair is what CodeQL flagged, and the check could always go stale before the operation — it never told us the read would succeed either.

The reads now go straight out through `readTextIfPresent`, which returns null **only** for ENOENT and rethrows everything else. That distinction is load-bearing: both callers of `readAlivePid` treat null as licence to act, so collapsing "unreadable" into "absent" means `ix view stop` deletes a live server's state and `ix view` spawns a second one it cannot record. `readRunningPort` keeps its swallow-all policy deliberately — it is looking up a URL to print, not liveness — and now says so. The scope read also stops reading a zero-length file as a workspace named `""`.

## #47 — `js/http-to-file-access` (medium), `ingest-baseline.ts`

The rev arrives off the backend's commit response and only the read side ever checked its shape, so a non-integer rev (an older backend answering `"9"` instead of `9`) cleared a bare `> 0` and was written, then rejected on the next read.

The save side is the *last* stop, though, not the first. The same value enters at the accumulator, where a bare `>` compares it as a string — `"9"` becomes the max, and `"10" > "9"` is then false, so the max walks backwards — and it ships to the user verbatim as the `latestRev` field of `ix ingest --format json`. `advanceRev` screens it where it enters, which fixes the max, the JSON contract and the persisted baseline in one place. `isRev` is now a single predicate both sides of the baseline share; they previously sat three lines apart and disagreed on whether 0 was valid.

To be accurate about the cost: `currentRev` is read only by `ix status`'s Revision line. Incremental skipping runs off the mtime map, which was always persisted correctly. A bad rev means a wrong Revision, **not** a re-ingest.

## #40 — Scorecard `Vulnerabilities` (high)

`nanoid` 3.3.16 → 3.3.18 and `brace-expansion` 5.0.7 → 5.0.9, clearing all three advisories behind the alert: GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8, GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg, GHSA-rgw5-rvv9-x895. Lockfiles only; both are dev-only transitive deps, and `npm audit` is clean in `ix-cli` and `core-ingestion`.

## Testing

`npm test` in `ix-cli`: 720 passed, 2 skipped. `npm run typecheck` clean; lint unchanged at 0 errors.

Every new assertion was checked against a restored mutant rather than assumed to be doing work. Swallowing all read errors brings back the orphan spawn (`spawn` called once, then EISDIR) and the silently-suppressed scope warning; `?? null` on the scope read brings back the bogus warning for an empty file; dropping the rev screen lets `"9"` win the max. Five mutants, five failures, then all pass.

The scope-mismatch branch previously had **no** coverage anywhere in the 713-test suite — every case seeded `compass.scope` as `"*all*"` and launched with `--all`, so the keys always matched and the warning never ran. It has a test now.

## Known leftovers

- `watch-utils.ts:readFileContent` still carries the same `existsSync`-then-read shape, plus an any-error-to-null contract that `watch` depends on. Left alone deliberately rather than widened into this PR.
- The temp-HOME test fixture is now duplicated in four test files and wants extracting into shared test support. Out of scope here.

## The other five alerts, for the record

- **#45, #46** (`js/http-to-file-access`, `view.ts`) — the same finding already dismissed as #28/#29. The flow is the `workspaceSystem` response reaching `systemId`; it is charset-constrained at `view.ts:309` and JSON-encoded at the sink, and the proxy has to embed its own scope. CodeQL keeps the taint because the guard tests the value rather than rebuilding it, which is correct of it and not worth laundering the code to satisfy.
- **#48** (Scorecard `PinnedDependencies`) — `skills/ix/scripts/bootstrap.sh` runs the official installer. Hash-pinning it would freeze bootstrap at one installer version and break on every release.
- **#39, #43** (Scorecard `SAST` / `CI-Tests`) — backward-looking scores over the last 30 merged PRs. CodeQL only began running on PR heads at #386; before that it ran on `main` pushes only, so the five uncovered PRs are already behind us. Both heal as PRs roll forward.

replacing the `existsSync` guards with bare `catch {}` made an unreadable
file indistinguishable from a missing one. Both callers of `readAlivePid`
treat null as licence to act, so that reads badly:

  then killed nothing.

its swallow-all policy on purpose and says why: it looks up a URL to print,
not liveness. The scope read also stops treating a zero-length file as a
workspace named "".

is read only by `ix status` — incremental skipping runs off the mtime map —
so a rejected rev costs a wrong Revision line, not a re-ingest. Comment and
test header corrected. More to the point the guard was at the last stop: the
value enters at the accumulator, where a bare `>` compares it as a string,
so "9" becomes the max and "10" > "9" is then false and the max walks
backwards. `advanceRev` screens it there, which fixes the max, the
`--format json` contract and the baseline at once. `isRev` is now one
predicate both sides share — they previously sat three lines apart and
disagreed on whether 0 was valid. `previousRev` is looked up lazily; it
parses the whole baseline, and `onCommitted` saves once per deleted file.

case seeded "*all*" and launched with --all), and the PID test asserted a
cleanup that cannot happen. Both replaced, plus the vacuous NaN case, which
passed against the bug. All five new assertions were checked against
restored mutants: swallow-all resurrects the orphan spawn and the silent
scope warning, and dropping the rev screen lets "9" win the max.

snapshot.title: fix(cli): register the patches command instead of stubbing it
snapshot.body:
## The bug

`ix-cli` has always contained a complete `ix patches` — client call, `--limit`, `--format text|json|llm`, and `formatPatches` already has a working `llm` branch (`format.ts:242`).

It was never imported by `register/oss.ts`. Meanwhile `patches` sat in `PRO_COMMANDS`, so `registerProStubs` installed the "requires Ix Pro" sentinel over the top of it.

So OSS users got a paywall message for a command this repo ships. Nobody noticed because the stub is a *plausible* answer — had it fallen through to commander's `unknown command` the way `goals` did (#384), it would have been reported long ago.

Found by @Alot1z while writing the agent skill (#368).

## The fix

Register it, and drop it from `PRO_COMMANDS`.

## The part worth reviewing

`@ix/pro` registers a `patches` too. Commander **throws** on a duplicate command name, and Pro's `tryRegister` wraps registration in a `try`/`catch` that swallows it — so on a Kartr install the OSS registration (which runs first, from `registerOssCommands`) is the one that survives, and Pro's is silently skipped.

That is the outcome we want: this version also supports `--format llm`, which Pro's does not. But it means the two implementations' behaviour now matters, so this one uses the same `createClient()` factory Pro's does instead of constructing `IxClient` directly. They are identical today (`createClient` is literally `new IxClient(getEndpoint())`) — the point is that its docstring says Pro commands should prefer it "so auth and endpoint resolution can evolve in one spot", and `patches` is now a command both editions route through.

Verified the swallow rather than assuming it: commander 12.1.0 raises `cannot add command 'patches' as already have command 'patches'` from `_registerCommand`, and `tryRegister`'s `catch` covers the `fn(program)` call, not just the `import`.

## Tests

The stub test asserting `patches` reports Pro is replaced by one asserting it is **not** stubbed. A stub for a command that exists in OSS shadows the real implementation, and because `registerOssCommands` runs first the symptom is silence, not a crash — worth pinning so it cannot come back.

722 tests green. `ix patches --help` verified against a real build.

## Docs

CLAUDE.md said the wrong thing in three places: the gotcha claiming `ix patches` is an unknown command, the `[Pro]` marker on its routing row, and the "only the first three work without Pro" line above that table.

Fixes #371

The stub test asserting `patches` reports Pro is replaced by one asserting it is **not** stubbed. A stub for a command that exists in OSS shadows the real implementation, and because `registerOssCommands` runs first the symptom is silence, not a crash — worth pinning so it cannot come back.

722 tests green. `ix patches --help` verified against a real build.

CLAUDE.md said the wrong thing in three places: the gotcha claiming `ix patches` is an unknown command, the `[Pro]` marker on its routing row, and the "only the first three work without Pro" line above that table.

Fixes #371

snapshot.title: fix(upgrade): stop comparing compass versions across two unrelated series
snapshot.body:
## The bug

`compass/.version` is written by two producers in two different version series, and recorded no way to tell them apart:

| producer | writes | series |
|---|---|---|
| `release.yml` | the **Ix** version (`0.9.2`) | Ix |
| `install.sh` / `install.ps1` / the compass-upgrade path | the **ix-compass-dist** release (`0.3.0`) | compass |

`isNewer(compassLatest, compassCurrent)` compared whichever happened to be on disk against the dist series. That is correct only while Ix's numbers are the larger ones. **The first ix-compass-dist tag above the running Ix version** — a v1.0.0, or just a v0.9.2 — makes `isNewer` true and replaces a *newer* bundled compass with an older dist build.

Same class as #365/#366, reached from the other end: there the stamp was missing so `current` read as `none`; here the stamp is present but denominated in the wrong series.

## It is not only latent

`install.sh` stamped every install with the latest **dist** release number regardless of where the compass came from. The compass it installs always comes from the release tarball — so it mislabelled a release bundle as a dist build, and clobbered the correct stamp the tarball already carried.

Reproduced on a live v0.9.x install:

```
~/.ix/cli/compass/.version   → 0.2.0     # written by install.sh, from ix-compass-dist
~/.ix/.version-check.json    → compassLatest: 0.3.0
```

`ix` prints "Compass update available" and `ix upgrade` would replace a bundle built from system-compass `main` at v0.9.x release time with dist v0.3.0.

## The fix

The stamp declares its own provenance, and the comparison only runs where it means something:

```
source=release        source=dist
ix=0.9.3              version=0.3.0
compass=7f98724
```

**A release bundle is never replaced by a dist download.** It was built from `main` when the CLI was cut, so it is at least as new as any dist release published before it; one published after arrives with the next Ix release, which bundles `main` again.

The dist download stays the **repair** path for a missing or gutted bundle. That still fires: `getInstalledCompassVersion()` reports `0.0.0` when `index.html` is absent, which no real release number matches.

## Backwards compatibility

A bare number is a legacy stamp — everything shipped up to and including v0.9.2 — and reads as **dist-series**. That is what `install.sh` wrote, it is the majority of installs in the wild, and it leaves them exactly as correct as they are today. Release-bundled legacy stamps stay accidentally-correct until compass-dist passes the Ix version, i.e. no worse than before. New releases carry the explicit form and are immune.

## Why the commit, not a version

`system-compass`'s `package.json` version is not maintained against the dist release series — it reads `0.2.0` while dist is on `v0.3.0` (built from `7f98724`). So stamping the package version would have been a third wrong number. The commit is the only reliable identity the bundle has, and it is passed from the `compass` job to `build` as a job output.

## Both installers stop calling ix-compass-dist

Neither ever installs from there, so neither needs to know what it has published. `resolve_compass_version` / `Get-CompassLatestVersion` are removed. `ix upgrade` asks that question, at the one point where it can also tell which series the installed bundle belongs to.

Each installer now prefers the stamp the tarball shipped with, and only writes one if the bundle has none.

## Tests

`upgrade-compass-stamp.test.ts` — release form, dist form, bare legacy number, empty/malformed, CRLF (how a Windows bundle arrives), and a case pinning the inversion itself.

728 tests green. `bash -n` and `sh -n` clean on install.sh; release.yml parses and `needs.compass.outputs.sha` resolves in the `build` job.

Fixes #376

when the CLI was cut, so it is at least as new as any dist release published
before it, and one published after arrives with the next Ix release, which
bundles `main` again. The dist download stays the *repair* path for a missing or
gutted bundle: that still fires, because `getInstalledCompassVersion()` reports
`0.0.0` when `index.html` is absent, which no real release number matches.

A bare number is a legacy stamp (everything up to v0.9.2) and reads as
dist-series — what install.sh wrote, the majority of installs in the wild, and
no less correct than today. New releases carry the explicit form and are immune.

The commit is recorded because system-compass's package.json version is not
maintained against the dist release series — it read 0.2.0 while dist was on
v0.3.0 — so the commit is the only reliable identity a bundle has.

Both installers stop asking ix-compass-dist what it has published. Neither ever
installs from there; `ix upgrade` asks that question, at the one point where it
can also tell which series the installed bundle belongs to.

Fixes #376

fix(upgrade): make the release-bundle guard reachable from a test

`shouldOfferCompassUpgrade` read the stamp itself, so the only thing the new
tests could reach was `parseCompassStamp`. Deleting the
`source === "release"` branch — the entire behavioural change in #376 — left
all 728 tests green while restoring the inversion in full.

Take the stamp as an argument and export the decision. `installedCompass()`
now returns the whole stamp instead of the version alone, which also stops
the function reading `compass/.version` twice per call.

Tests cover the inversion itself, the dist-series comparison that must still
happen, the repair path for a gutted bundle (which is why the 0.0.0 check
sits ahead of the source check — reversing them is #365/#366 again), the
offline case, and a legacy bare stamp. Both mutations now fail the suite.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(upgrade): keep the compass stamp readable by already-shipped CLIs

The key=value stamp is unreadable by every CLI already in the wild, and the
shipped CLI is exactly what reads it during the upgrade that installs it:
`ix upgrade` swaps in the new tree, then the still-running old process
continues into its own compass block and reads the file it just wrote.

That reader is getTrackedVersion — readFileSync(...).trim(), the whole file —
feeding splitVersion. Measured against origin/main's own isNewer:

  dist 0.3.0 vs "source=release\nix=0.9.4\n..."  -> false  (garbled print)
  dist 0.3.0 vs "source=release\nix=1.0.0\n..."  -> TRUE
  dist 0.3.0 vs "source=release\nix=1.1.0\n..."  -> TRUE

The major parses as NaN -> 0, so at the first 1.x release every older CLI
downloads ix-compass-dist over the newer bundle it just installed — #376
reintroduced by the format change itself.

Provenance now rides in semver build metadata on one line:

  0.9.3+release.7f98724     release bundle
  0.3.0                     dist download (bare, as it has always been)

behave exactly as they do today.

Also from the same review:

- `present` (index.html on disk) replaces version "0.0.0" as the repair
  trigger. 0.0.0 is also what a stamp truncated by a full disk parses to, and
  repairing on that downgrades an intact release bundle.
- install.sh only stamps when it actually extracted the tarball. The block
  runs even when the install was skipped, where the compass on disk can be an
  unstamped *dist* bundle — labelling that `+release` froze it against every
  future compass update. When we did extract, the tarball's own stamp has
  already landed and repairs a mislabelled install.
- New producer drift test: reads release.yml, install.sh and install.ps1,
  renders each stamp literal and pushes it through the real parser. Three
  producers in three languages with no compile-time link to the reader is how
  this class of bug keeps happening. Verified non-vacuous — restoring the
  multi-line form fails both properties.

744 green. bash -n / sh -n clean, release.yml parses, install.ps1 parses.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

The diagnosis is right and the live reproduction settles it — `.version` really was denominated in the wrong series, and `source=` is the correct shape for the answer. Checked the parts that could bite:

- `build` does declare `needs: compass`, so `needs.compass.outputs.sha` resolves; on a PR dry-run compass is skipped and the `${COMPASS_SHA:-unknown}` fallback covers it.
- No leftover callers of `resolve_compass_version` / `Get-CompassLatestVersion` — both survive only as comments.
- `$Version` is assigned at `install.ps1:207`, well above the stamp block at :532.
- The `0.0.0` repair check correctly sits *ahead* of the source check, so a gutted release bundle is still repaired rather than pinned forever.

**One gap, fixed in c415461.** `shouldOfferCompassUpgrade` read the stamp itself, so the only thing the new test file could reach was `parseCompassStamp` — a pure function that was never the bug. I deleted the `readCompassStamp().source === "release"` line, which is the entire behavioural change here, and all 728 tests passed. The case named `pins the inversion the marker exists to prevent` survives it too: `expect(parseCompassStamp(...).source).toBe("release")` restates the parser rather than the decision.

Made the decision take the stamp as an argument (`shouldOfferCompassUpgradeFor`) and exported it. `installedCompass()` now returns the whole stamp rather than the version alone, which also drops a second read of `compass/.version` per call.

Five cases now cover it: the inversion, the dist-series comparison that must still happen, the repair path for a gutted bundle, the offline case, and a legacy bare stamp. Two mutations verified failing — deleting the source check, and swapping it ahead of the `0.0.0` check (that one is #365/#366 again: `ix view` never repairs).

733 green.

Retracting my earlier approval. A deeper review turned up a blocking backward-compatibility break that I verified empirically, so this should not merge in its current form.

## Blocking: the new stamp format is unreadable by every already-shipped CLI

The shipped reader is `getTrackedVersion` (`upgrade.ts:199-206`) — `readFileSync(...).trim()`, i.e. **the whole file**. The upgrade sequence matters here: `ix upgrade` swaps in the new tree (including the new-format `compass/.version`), and then the *still-running old process* continues into its own compass block and reads that file with the old parser.

I ran the new format through `origin/main`'s own `isNewer`:

```
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 0.9.4 -> isNewer=false
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 1.0.0 -> isNewer=TRUE
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 1.1.0 -> isNewer=TRUE
dist 0.3.0 vs legacy bare  0.9.4 -> isNewer=false
```

`splitVersion` yields `Number("source=release\nix=1") = NaN -> 0` for the major, so a 1.x release parses as `[0,0,0]`. Today (0.9.x) the damage is a garbled three-line version string in `[ok] Compass already on the latest version (...)`. **At the first 1.0.0 release, every CLI older than this one downloads ix-compass-dist over the newer bundled compass** — the exact #376 downgrade this PR exists to prevent, caused by the format change itself.

Suggested fix that keeps the whole design: make the stamp a **single-line semver with build metadata**, `0.9.4+release.7f98724`. `splitVersion` already does `v.split("+")[0]` with the comment "Build metadata (`+sha`) never participates in precedence" — so old CLIs read `0.9.4` and behave exactly as they do today, while `parseCompassStamp` reads the `+release.<sha>` suffix for provenance. Dist stays a bare number, which is already the legacy-compatible form.

## Also blocking

**`0.0.0` is overloaded** (`upgrade.ts:298`). The doc comment says only a missing `index.html` produces it, but `parseCompassStamp` also returns `{source:"release", version:"0.0.0"}` for a release stamp missing its `ix=` key — a `.version` truncated by a full disk or a kill during the non-atomic write. With the bundle perfectly serviceable, the repair branch fires ahead of the source check and downgrades it. Worth distinguishing "absent" from "malformed" explicitly rather than through the version number.

**`install.sh:1094` stamps `source=release` on a compass it did not install.** The stamp block runs even when the CLI install was skipped (`check_installed_version` == `$VERSION`, or `SKIP_CLI_INSTALL=1`). If `compass/` holds an unstamped *dist* bundle — reachable via `ix upgrade`'s own `stage="stamp"` failure, or Ctrl-C between extract and stamp — it is now permanently labelled `release`, and `shouldOfferCompassUpgradeFor` refuses every future compass update while printing "Compass is the build bundled with Ix <v>", which is false. The deleted code re-stamped with the dist number and stayed self-correcting.

**`install.sh:1093`'s `[ ! -s .version ]` never repairs a mislabelled stamp** — so the fix does not reach the installs the PR body calls the majority in the wild. Re-running the installer on an already-current version skips the extract, so no tarball stamp is laid down, and the bare `0.3.0` survives.

**`IX_VERSION=0.9.0` pins** stamp `source=release ix=0.9.0` onto a months-old bundle and exempt it from dist upgrades forever. `resolve_version` also falls back to `0.1.0` when the API is unreachable.

## Non-blocking

Gating the compass block behind `shouldOfferCompassUpgrade` also gates the orphan sweep inside it. `main` has exactly two sweep sites — one behind "CLI needs updating", one behind "compass needs updating" — and the second exists as the fallback for the first, per its own comment. After this change a user on the latest CLI with a release compass sweeps nothing. I traced it and the severe cases self-heal (a gutted compass reports 0.0.0 and repairs; an interrupted CLI upgrade leaves the CLI stale), so this is stranded orphan directories rather than breakage — but it undercuts #392's reason for sweeping downloads at all.

The diagnosis and the live reproduction in the PR body are right, and the provenance idea is the correct answer. It is the encoding that needs to change.

Addressed in 3f70e75. Re-verified end to end.

**Stamp format.** Provenance now rides in semver build metadata on one line — `0.9.3+release.7f98724` for a release bundle, a bare number for dist. `splitVersion` already drops everything after `+`, so every already-shipped CLI reads `0.9.3` and behaves exactly as it does today. The design intent is unchanged; only the encoding moved.

**`present` replaces the `0.0.0` sentinel.** `installedCompass()` carries whether `index.html` is on disk, so a stamp truncated mid-write no longer masquerades as a missing bundle and triggers a downgrade of an intact one. snapshot.title: fix(upgrade): stop comparing compass versions across two unrelated series
snapshot.body:
## The bug

`compass/.version` is written by two producers in two different version series, and recorded no way to tell them apart:

| producer | writes | series |
|---|---|---|
| `release.yml` | the **Ix** version (`0.9.2`) | Ix |
| `install.sh` / `install.ps1` / the compass-upgrade path | the **ix-compass-dist** release (`0.3.0`) | compass |

`isNewer(compassLatest, compassCurrent)` compared whichever happened to be on disk against the dist series. That is correct only while Ix's numbers are the larger ones. **The first ix-compass-dist tag above the running Ix version** — a v1.0.0, or just a v0.9.2 — makes `isNewer` true and replaces a *newer* bundled compass with an older dist build.

Same class as #365/#366, reached from the other end: there the stamp was missing so `current` read as `none`; here the stamp is present but denominated in the wrong series.

## It is not only latent

`install.sh` stamped every install with the latest **dist** release number regardless of where the compass came from. The compass it installs always comes from the release tarball — so it mislabelled a release bundle as a dist build, and clobbered the correct stamp the tarball already carried.

Reproduced on a live v0.9.x install:

```
~/.ix/cli/compass/.version   → 0.2.0     # written by install.sh, from ix-compass-dist
~/.ix/.version-check.json    → compassLatest: 0.3.0
```

`ix` prints "Compass update available" and `ix upgrade` would replace a bundle built from system-compass `main` at v0.9.x release time with dist v0.3.0.

## The fix

The stamp declares its own provenance, and the comparison only runs where it means something:

```
source=release        source=dist
ix=0.9.3              version=0.3.0
compass=7f98724
```

**A release bundle is never replaced by a dist download.** It was built from `main` when the CLI was cut, so it is at least as new as any dist release published before it; one published after arrives with the next Ix release, which bundles `main` again.

The dist download stays the **repair** path for a missing or gutted bundle. That still fires: `getInstalledCompassVersion()` reports `0.0.0` when `index.html` is absent, which no real release number matches.

## Backwards compatibility

A bare number is a legacy stamp — everything shipped up to and including v0.9.2 — and reads as **dist-series**. That is what `install.sh` wrote, it is the majority of installs in the wild, and it leaves them exactly as correct as they are today. Release-bundled legacy stamps stay accidentally-correct until compass-dist passes the Ix version, i.e. no worse than before. New releases carry the explicit form and are immune.

## Why the commit, not a version

`system-compass`'s `package.json` version is not maintained against the dist release series — it reads `0.2.0` while dist is on `v0.3.0` (built from `7f98724`). So stamping the package version would have been a third wrong number. The commit is the only reliable identity the bundle has, and it is passed from the `compass` job to `build` as a job output.

## Both installers stop calling ix-compass-dist

Neither ever installs from there, so neither needs to know what it has published. `resolve_compass_version` / `Get-CompassLatestVersion` are removed. `ix upgrade` asks that question, at the one point where it can also tell which series the installed bundle belongs to.

Each installer now prefers the stamp the tarball shipped with, and only writes one if the bundle has none.

## Tests

`upgrade-compass-stamp.test.ts` — release form, dist form, bare legacy number, empty/malformed, CRLF (how a Windows bundle arrives), and a case pinning the inversion itself.

728 tests green. `bash -n` and `sh -n` clean on install.sh; release.yml parses and `needs.compass.outputs.sha` resolves in the `build` job.

Fixes #376

installs from there; `ix upgrade` asks that question, at the one point where it
can also tell which series the installed bundle belongs to.

Fixes #376

fix(upgrade): make the release-bundle guard reachable from a test

`shouldOfferCompassUpgrade` read the stamp itself, so the only thing the new
tests could reach was `parseCompassStamp`. Deleting the
`source === "release"` branch — the entire behavioural change in #376 — left
all 728 tests green while restoring the inversion in full.

Take the stamp as an argument and export the decision. `installedCompass()`
now returns the whole stamp instead of the version alone, which also stops
the function reading `compass/.version` twice per call.

Tests cover the inversion itself, the dist-series comparison that must still
happen, the repair path for a gutted bundle (which is why the 0.0.0 check
sits ahead of the source check — reversing them is #365/#366 again), the
offline case, and a legacy bare stamp. Both mutations now fail the suite.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(upgrade): keep the compass stamp readable by already-shipped CLIs

The key=value stamp is unreadable by every CLI already in the wild, and the
shipped CLI is exactly what reads it during the upgrade that installs it:
`ix upgrade` swaps in the new tree, then the still-running old process
continues into its own compass block and reads the file it just wrote.

That reader is getTrackedVersion — readFileSync(...).trim(), the whole file —
feeding splitVersion. Measured against origin/main's own isNewer:

  dist 0.3.0 vs "source=release\nix=0.9.4\n..."  -> false  (garbled print)
  dist 0.3.0 vs "source=release\nix=1.0.0\n..."  -> TRUE
  dist 0.3.0 vs "source=release\nix=1.1.0\n..."  -> TRUE

The major parses as NaN -> 0, so at the first 1.x release every older CLI
downloads ix-compass-dist over the newer bundle it just installed — #376
reintroduced by the format change itself.

Provenance now rides in semver build metadata on one line:

  0.9.3+release.7f98724     release bundle
  0.3.0                     dist download (bare, as it has always been)
