behave exactly as they do today.

Also from the same review:

- `present` (index.html on disk) replaces version "0.0.0" as the repair
  trigger. 0.0.0 is also what a stamp truncated by a full disk parses to, and
  repairing on that downgrades an intact release bundle.
- install.sh only stamps when it actually extracted the tarball. The block
  runs even when the install was skipped, where the compass on disk can be an
  unstamped *dist* bundle — labelling that `+release` froze it against every
  future compass update. When we did extract, the tarball's own stamp has
  already landed and repairs a mislabelled install.
- New producer drift test: reads release.yml, install.sh and install.ps1,
  renders each stamp literal and pushes it through the real parser. Three
  producers in three languages with no compile-time link to the reader is how
  this class of bug keeps happening. Verified non-vacuous — restoring the
  multi-line form fails both properties.

744 green. bash -n / sh -n clean, release.yml parses, install.ps1 parses.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

reviews.body:
The diagnosis is right and the live reproduction settles it — `.version` really was denominated in the wrong series, and `source=` is the correct shape for the answer. Checked the parts that could bite:

- `build` does declare `needs: compass`, so `needs.compass.outputs.sha` resolves; on a PR dry-run compass is skipped and the `${COMPASS_SHA:-unknown}` fallback covers it.
- No leftover callers of `resolve_compass_version` / `Get-CompassLatestVersion` — both survive only as comments.
- `$Version` is assigned at `install.ps1:207`, well above the stamp block at :532.
- The `0.0.0` repair check correctly sits *ahead* of the source check, so a gutted release bundle is still repaired rather than pinned forever.

**One gap, fixed in c415461.** `shouldOfferCompassUpgrade` read the stamp itself, so the only thing the new test file could reach was `parseCompassStamp` — a pure function that was never the bug. I deleted the `readCompassStamp().source === "release"` line, which is the entire behavioural change here, and all 728 tests passed. The case named `pins the inversion the marker exists to prevent` survives it too: `expect(parseCompassStamp(...).source).toBe("release")` restates the parser rather than the decision.

Made the decision take the stamp as an argument (`shouldOfferCompassUpgradeFor`) and exported it. `installedCompass()` now returns the whole stamp rather than the version alone, which also drops a second read of `compass/.version` per call.

Five cases now cover it: the inversion, the dist-series comparison that must still happen, the repair path for a gutted bundle, the offline case, and a legacy bare stamp. Two mutations verified failing — deleting the source check, and swapping it ahead of the `0.0.0` check (that one is #365/#366 again: `ix view` never repairs).

733 green.

Retracting my earlier approval. A deeper review turned up a blocking backward-compatibility break that I verified empirically, so this should not merge in its current form.

## Blocking: the new stamp format is unreadable by every already-shipped CLI

The shipped reader is `getTrackedVersion` (`upgrade.ts:199-206`) — `readFileSync(...).trim()`, i.e. **the whole file**. The upgrade sequence matters here: `ix upgrade` swaps in the new tree (including the new-format `compass/.version`), and then the *still-running old process* continues into its own compass block and reads that file with the old parser.

I ran the new format through `origin/main`'s own `isNewer`:

```
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 0.9.4 -> isNewer=false
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 1.0.0 -> isNewer=TRUE
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 1.1.0 -> isNewer=TRUE
dist 0.3.0 vs legacy bare  0.9.4 -> isNewer=false
```

`splitVersion` yields `Number("source=release\nix=1") = NaN -> 0` for the major, so a 1.x release parses as `[0,0,0]`. Today (0.9.x) the damage is a garbled three-line version string in `[ok] Compass already on the latest version (...)`. **At the first 1.0.0 release, every CLI older than this one downloads ix-compass-dist over the newer bundled compass** — the exact #376 downgrade this PR exists to prevent, caused by the format change itself.

Suggested fix that keeps the whole design: make the stamp a **single-line semver with build metadata**, `0.9.4+release.7f98724`. `splitVersion` already does `v.split("+")[0]` with the comment "Build metadata (`+sha`) never participates in precedence" — so old CLIs read `0.9.4` and behave exactly as they do today, while `parseCompassStamp` reads the `+release.<sha>` suffix for provenance. Dist stays a bare number, which is already the legacy-compatible form.

## Also blocking

**`0.0.0` is overloaded** (`upgrade.ts:298`). The doc comment says only a missing `index.html` produces it, but `parseCompassStamp` also returns `{source:"release", version:"0.0.0"}` for a release stamp missing its `ix=` key — a `.version` truncated by a full disk or a kill during the non-atomic write. With the bundle perfectly serviceable, the repair branch fires ahead of the source check and downgrades it. Worth distinguishing "absent" from "malformed" explicitly rather than through the version number.

**`install.sh:1094` stamps `source=release` on a compass it did not install.** The stamp block runs even when the CLI install was skipped (`check_installed_version` == `$VERSION`, or `SKIP_CLI_INSTALL=1`). If `compass/` holds an unstamped *dist* bundle — reachable via `ix upgrade`'s own `stage="stamp"` failure, or Ctrl-C between extract and stamp — it is now permanently labelled `release`, and `shouldOfferCompassUpgradeFor` refuses every future compass update while printing "Compass is the build bundled with Ix <v>", which is false. The deleted code re-stamped with the dist number and stayed self-correcting.

**`install.sh:1093`'s `[ ! -s .version ]` never repairs a mislabelled stamp** — so the fix does not reach the installs the PR body calls the majority in the wild. Re-running the installer on an already-current version skips the extract, so no tarball stamp is laid down, and the bare `0.3.0` survives.

**`IX_VERSION=0.9.0` pins** stamp `source=release ix=0.9.0` onto a months-old bundle and exempt it from dist upgrades forever. `resolve_version` also falls back to `0.1.0` when the API is unreachable.

## Non-blocking

Gating the compass block behind `shouldOfferCompassUpgrade` also gates the orphan sweep inside it. `main` has exactly two sweep sites — one behind "CLI needs updating", one behind "compass needs updating" — and the second exists as the fallback for the first, per its own comment. After this change a user on the latest CLI with a release compass sweeps nothing. I traced it and the severe cases self-heal (a gutted compass reports 0.0.0 and repairs; an interrupted CLI upgrade leaves the CLI stale), so this is stranded orphan directories rather than breakage — but it undercuts #392's reason for sweeping downloads at all.

The diagnosis and the live reproduction in the PR body are right, and the provenance idea is the correct answer. It is the encoding that needs to change.

Addressed in 3f70e75. Re-verified end to end.

**Stamp format.** Provenance now rides in semver build metadata on one line — `0.9.3+release.7f98724` for a release bundle, a bare number for dist. `splitVersion` already drops everything after `+`, so every already-shipped CLI reads `0.9.3` and behaves exactly as it does today. The design intent is unchanged; only the encoding moved.

**`present` replaces the `0.0.0` sentinel.** `installedCompass()` carries whether `index.html` is on disk, so a stamp truncated mid-write no longer masquerades as a missing bundle and triggers a downgrade of an intact one. The present-check still sits ahead of the source-check, so a gutted release bundle is repaired.

**install.sh only stamps what it installed.** Gated on a new `CLI_EXTRACTED` flag. The block runs even when the install was skipped, and in that case the compass on disk can be an unstamped dist bundle — labelling that `+release` froze it against every future update. When we did extract, the tarball's own stamp has already landed, which is also what repairs a mislabelled install. `install.ps1` needs no such gate: it has no already-current skip path.

**New producer drift test.** `upgrade-compass-stamp-producers.test.ts` reads `release.yml`, `install.sh` and `install.ps1`, renders the literal each one writes, and pushes it through the real `parseCompassStamp`. Three producers in three languages with no compile-time link to the reader is how this class of bug keeps recurring. Verified non-vacuous — restoring the multi-line form fails both properties it asserts.

Mutations re-run against the reworked code: deleting the release guard fails two cases, and reverting the stamp producer fails two more.

744 green. `bash -n` and `sh -n` clean on install.sh, release.yml parses, install.ps1 parses clean.

Left as-is deliberately: an `IX_VERSION` pin stamps `+release` on that release's bundle and exempts it from dist upgrades. That reads correct to me — the user pinned a release, and the repair path still fires if the bundle is gutted — but flagging it since the review raised it.

snapshot.title: fix(upgrade): stage downloads under IX_HOME, not TEMP
snapshot.body:
## Why

#349 is a Windows install that died after extraction because TEMP arrived in 8.3 short form (`C:\Users\WIN10\~1\...`) on a profile named `C:\Users\Win 10`. The reporter confirmed that pointing `TEMP`/`TMP` at a path without a space let the same install finish.

#352 moved `install.ps1`'s scratch off TEMP for that reason — and said so in its own comment:

> Note `ix upgrade` still stages through `os.tmpdir()` (upgrade.ts), which on Windows is TEMP verbatim. If this class is real, it is unfixed there.

This is that half. It is the worse of the two places for the failure to bite: a failed install leaves a machine with no Ix on it, but a **failed upgrade breaks an install that was working** — which is exactly the shape of #385.

## What changed

Both download directories move to `IX_HOME`, joining the staging and backup directories already there. `IX_HOME` comes from `USERPROFILE` in its long form. `mkdirSync(IX_HOME)` first, because a first upgrade after a manual install can reach this before anything has created it.

`sweepUpgradeOrphans` learns `.cli-download-` and `.compass-download-`. Leaving TEMP also leaves the OS's own cleanup, so without this an upgrade killed mid-download parks a multi-MB archive in `~/.ix` forever.

The prefixes are deliberately `-download-` and not `-backup-`: `recover()` renames the newest `.cli-backup-*` over the install directory, and an archive must never be a candidate for that. There is already a test pinning that reasoning for `install.ps1`'s zip; this adds the matching one.

## The part I nearly broke

**The sweep call had to move above the download.** It sat between the download and the extract, which was safe only while the scratch lived in `os.tmpdir()`. Once the sweep reclaims `.cli-download-*`, from that position it deletes the archive it is about to extract — breaking *every* upgrade on every platform, not just Windows.

Caught while tracing the ordering rather than by a test, so there is now a test for it. Above the download, the sweep also puts an interrupted install back even when the download then fails, which the old order could not do. The compass branch already had this ordering; the CLI branch was the odd one out.

## Tests

724 green. Two new cases: an interrupted download's scratch is reclaimed, and a download directory is not treated as an install worth recovering.

`npm run lint` — 0 errors (38 pre-existing warnings). The now-unused `tmpdir` import is dropped.

## Not verified

No Windows machine here, so the 8.3 path itself is still unreproduced — see the note on #349 about the mechanism never having been pinned down. What this does is take the upgrade path off TEMP entirely, which fixes the failure under every reading of it.

Refs #349

fix(upgrade): bound the sweep's new reach into IX_HOME

range, and hoisting the sweep above the download made its destructive half
run on upgrades that install nothing. Two consequences, both new:

**A failed download could delete the only working compass.**
cleanupCompassSwap:615 tests `index.html` rather than a bare existsSync, and
its comment says why: a compass/ holding only a .version is a real state, and
a bare existsSync "would call that 'back in place' and drop a backup the
caller had just told the user to go and rescue". recover() used exactly that
bare test, so the two disagreed on precisely that state — recover declined to
restore over the husk, then the loop deleted the backup. Preserved by the
swap's cleanup, destroyed by the sweep. On main this only fired after a
successful download; above the download, an offline `ix upgrade` was enough.

reviews.body:
Taking the upgrade path off TEMP is right, and the reasoning for `-download-` over `-backup-` is correct — `recover()` renames the newest `.cli-backup-*` over the install directory, so an archive must never match that prefix.

**One gap, fixed in c8754ba.** The PR calls the sweep-above-download move "the part I nearly broke" and says "there is now a test for it". There wasn't. The two new cases pin *which prefixes the sweep reclaims*, which is what makes the ordering matter, but not the ordering itself — that lived inline in the command action where no test reaches it. I moved the call back below the download and all 724 tests passed, on a change that breaks every upgrade on every platform because the sweep then deletes the archive it is about to extract.

Both call sites now go through `prepareDownloadDir(ixHome, installDir, prefix)`, which does mkdir → sweep → mkdtemp. The order is inside one testable function instead of duplicated across two sites as a comment. Three cases: an earlier run's scratch is reclaimed while the one just created survives, an interrupted install is restored before any download happens, and IX_HOME is created when a manual install never did. Inverting the order inside the helper fails all three.

Worth noting the compass branch got the same treatment, so it no longer sweeps and then separately mkdirs — one shape on both paths.

727 green, lint clean.

Retracting my earlier approval — a deeper review found two correctness regressions introduced by moving the scratch into `IX_HOME`, one of which is data loss.

## Blocking: a failed download can delete the user's only working compass

`cleanupCompassSwap:615` tests `existsSync(join(compassDir, "index.html"))` and its comment is explicit about why: a `compass/` holding only a `.version` is a real state, and a bare `existsSync` "would call that 'back in place' and drop a backup the caller had just told the user to go and rescue."

`recover()` inside `sweepUpgradeOrphans` uses exactly that bare `existsSync(dest)`. So with `compass/` left as a `.version`-only husk and `.compass-backup-1234` holding the only real bundle, `recover()` declines to restore, and the loop below then deletes the backup.

On `main` that sweep ran *after* a successful download, so an offline run exited before reaching it and the backup survived for the next attempt. Hoisting the sweep above `curl` means **a run that installs nothing now destroys it** — the user sees only "[error] Failed to download", and `ix view` is permanently blank with no copy left on disk.

The two tests can't see this because they never construct the husk. Aligning `recover`'s test with `cleanupCompassSwap`'s (`index.html`, not bare `existsSync`) fixes it and makes the two agree.

## Blocking: concurrent `ix upgrade` deletes an in-flight download

The scratch moved from `os.tmpdir()`, where no sweep could match it, into `IX_HOME` with a swept prefix. Process A creates `.cli-download-AAAAAA` and starts a curl with a 300s timeout; process B — a second terminal, or `bootstrap.sh` re-running `ix upgrade` when it finds compass missing — calls `prepareDownloadDir` and deletes A's directory wholesale. On Linux/macOS curl's fd stays valid so A exits 0, then `tar -xzf` hits a missing path and A reports "Failed to extract CLI update" on a good download.

`.cli-staging-<pid>` has the same shape on main, but its window is the few seconds of extraction; this one is the whole download. Some ownership marker (pid in the name, skipped when that pid is live) would close both.

## Worth addressing

- `prepareDownloadDir` in the compass branch is the first filesystem write under `IX_HOME` and sits *outside* the try/catch that deliberately keeps compass failures non-fatal. On an unwritable `~/.ix` this turns "[!!] Compass extract failed / ix view keeps working" into a hard abort that also skips `writeCache`.
- Two bare `rmSync` calls (959, 1264) skip the retry treatment `rmQuiet` exists for — and this PR moves those directories into the user profile, where AV and indexer handles are the norm, which is precisely the case `rmQuiet`'s comment describes.

## One question before this lands

#349's reporter is on `C:\Users\Win 10` and their confirmed workaround was pointing TEMP at a space-free path. This moves the scratch from `C:\Users\WIN10~1\AppData\Local\Temp\...` (no space — 8.3 aliases never contain one) to `C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\.cli-download-...` (space). If the failure is space-driven rather than short-path-driven, the upgrade path now has the space where it previously didn't. "Refs #349" rather than "Fixes" is the right call, and the PR is honest that it's unreproduced — but "fixes the failure under every reading of it" doesn't hold under the space reading. Nothing in the suite sets `IX_HOME` to a path with a space.

Taking the upgrade path off TEMP is still right, and the `-download-` vs `-backup-` prefix reasoning is correct. It's the sweep's new reach that needs bounding.

Addressed in 5432c49 and b4d9c00, and rebased onto main now that #391 has landed.

**The data-loss path.** `recover()` now takes the file that proves the thing is real — `index.html` for the compass, `cli/dist/cli/main.js` for the install — so it applies the same test `cleanupCompassSwap` already applies. The two no longer disagree about a husk, so a torn swap restores the backup instead of the sweep deleting it. Verified: reverting to the bare `existsSync` fails two of the new cases.

**The concurrency window.** Download directories carry their pid (`.cli-download-<pid>-<rand>`) and the sweep skips one whose process is still addressable — `process.kill(pid, 0)`, treating EPERM as live. Unparseable names are treated as dead so the pre-pid naming stays collectable, and the guard is scoped to download prefixes so staging/backup reclaim behaviour is untouched. Verified: removing the guard fails the live-process case.

**The two bare `rmSync` calls** are now `rmQuiet`, which is the whole reason that helper exists — and this PR is what moves those directories from TEMP into the user profile.

**One more, found while composing the two PRs** (b4d9c00): both sweep calls sit behind "something needs updating", and #391 tightened the compass gate to skip release-bundled compasses — which is every install from v0.9.3 on. So on a healthy current install neither would fire and nothing would ever be reclaimed, which defeats the reason for sweeping the downloads at all. There is now one unconditional sweep at the top of a real `ix upgrade`; the calls inside `prepareDownloadDir` stay, since that is where the ordering invariant lives.

753 green on the rebased result, lint clean.

**Still open, and deliberately not resolved here:** whether #349 is space-driven or short-path-driven. The scratch now sits under `C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\...`, which contains the space, where the TEMP path it replaces did not. `Refs #349` is the right framing until someone reproduces it — worth keeping the issue open rather than closing it on this.

commits.message:
fix(upgrade): stage downloads under IX_HOME, not TEMP

#349 is a Windows install that died after extraction because TEMP arrived in
8.3 short form (`C:\Users\WIN10\~1\...`) on a profile named `C:\Users\Win 10`;
the reporter confirmed that pointing TEMP and TMP at a path without a space let
the same install finish. #352 moved install.ps1's scratch off TEMP for that
reason, and said in its own comment that `ix upgrade` still stages through
`os.tmpdir()` — which on Windows is TEMP verbatim — so if the class is real it
is unfixed there.

It is the worse of the two places for it to bite: a failed install leaves a
machine with no Ix on it, but a failed upgrade breaks an install that was
working.

Both download directories move to `IX_HOME`, which comes from USERPROFILE in
its long form, joining the staging and backup directories that were already
there. `mkdirSync(IX_HOME)` first, because a first upgrade after a manual
install may reach this before anything has created it.

Leaving TEMP also leaves the OS's own cleanup, so `sweepUpgradeOrphans` learns
the two new prefixes — otherwise an upgrade killed mid-download parks a
multi-MB archive in ~/.ix forever. They are deliberately `-download-` and not
`-backup-`: `recover()` renames the newest `.cli-backup-*` over the install
directory, and an archive must never be a candidate for that.

**The sweep call had to move above the download.** It sat between the download
and the extract, which was safe only while the scratch lived in os.tmpdir();
now that the sweep reclaims `.cli-download-*`, from that position it would
delete the archive it was about to extract and break every upgrade. Above the
download it also puts an interrupted install back even when the download then
fails, which the old order could not do. The compass branch already had this
ordering.

Refs #349

fix(upgrade): make the sweep-before-download order structural, not a comment

The PR notes the sweep call had to move above the download and says there is
now a test for it. There was not: the two new cases pin which prefixes the
sweep reclaims, but the ordering lived inline in the command action where no
test could reach it. Moving the call back below the download — which breaks
every upgrade on every platform, since the sweep then deletes the archive it
is about to extract — left all 724 tests passing.

Both call sites now go through `prepareDownloadDir()`, which does mkdir,
sweep, mkdtemp in that order and is directly testable. Three cases cover it:
an earlier run's scratch is reclaimed while the new one survives, an
interrupted install is restored before any download happens, and IX_HOME is
created when a manual install never did. Inverting the order inside the
helper fails all three.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(upgrade): bound the sweep's new reach into IX_HOME

Moving the download scratch under IX_HOME put it inside sweepUpgradeOrphans'
range, and hoisting the sweep above the download made its destructive half
run on upgrades that install nothing. Two consequences, both new:

**A failed download could delete the only working compass.**
cleanupCompassSwap:615 tests `index.html` rather than a bare existsSync, and
its comment says why: a compass/ holding only a .version is a real state, and
a bare existsSync "would call that 'back in place' and drop a backup the
caller had just told the user to go and rescue". recover() used exactly that
bare test, so the two disagreed on precisely that state — recover declined to
restore over the husk, then the loop deleted the backup. Preserved by the
swap's cleanup, destroyed by the sweep. On main this only fired after a
successful download; above the download, an offline `ix upgrade` was enough.

recover() now takes the file that proves the thing is real — index.html for
the compass, dist/cli/main.js for the install — so the two agree.

**A concurrent `ix upgrade` deleted the first run's in-flight download.**
The scratch used to live in os.tmpdir() where no sweep could match it; under
IX_HOME it was collectable for the whole 300s curl timeout. A second terminal,
or bootstrap.sh re-running `ix upgrade` when it finds compass missing, would
remove the archive mid-download — and on POSIX the unlink is silent and curl
still exits 0, so the victim fails at the extract on a download it completed.

Download directories now carry their pid (`.cli-download-<pid>-<rand>`) and
the sweep skips one whose process is still addressable. Unparseable names are
treated as dead so the pre-pid naming stays collectable. Downloads only —
staging/backup carry no pid and their reclaim behaviour is left alone.

Also: the two bare rmSync calls become rmQuiet. rmQuiet exists because Windows
rmSync does not retry and "an AV or indexer handle ... is enough to throw" —
and this PR moves those directories from TEMP into the user profile, where
scanning and indexing are the norm. The compass one runs on the success path,
where a throw skips writeCache and leaves the update notice firing for the
version just installed.

Six new cases, each verified against its bug: reverting recover() to the bare
existsSync fails two, and removing the live-pid guard fails another.

732 green, lint clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(upgrade): sweep orphans on every upgrade, not only when one is available

Both sweep calls sit behind "something needs updating" — one inside the CLI
branch, one inside the compass branch, the latter existing precisely as the
fallback for the former. #376 then tightened the compass gate to skip
release-bundled compasses, which is every install from v0.9.3 on. So a user on
the latest CLI with a release compass now runs `ix upgrade` and reclaims
nothing, and an interrupted swap is never restored.

That matters most for this PR: the archives it teaches the sweep about are
multi-MB, and the stated reason for sweeping them is that leaving os.tmpdir()
also left the OS's own cleanup. A sweep that only runs when an update happens
to be available does not deliver that.

One readdir of ~/.ix when there is nothing to do. The calls inside
prepareDownloadDir stay — that is where the sweep-before-scratch ordering is
enforced — and simply find nothing.

753 green, lint clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

reviews.body:
Taking the upgrade path off TEMP is right, and the reasoning for `-download-` over `-backup-` is correct — `recover()` renames the newest `.cli-backup-*` over the install directory, so an archive must never match that prefix.

**One gap, fixed in c8754ba.** The PR calls the sweep-above-download move "the part I nearly broke" and says "there is now a test for it". There wasn't. The two new cases pin *which prefixes the sweep reclaims*, which is what makes the ordering matter, but not the ordering itself — that lived inline in the command action where no test reaches it. I moved the call back below the download and all 724 tests passed, on a change that breaks every upgrade on every platform because the sweep then deletes the archive it is about to extract.

Both call sites now go through `prepareDownloadDir(ixHome, installDir, prefix)`, which does mkdir → sweep → mkdtemp. The order is inside one testable function instead of duplicated across two sites as a comment. Three cases: an earlier run's scratch is reclaimed while the one just created survives, an interrupted install is restored before any download happens, and IX_HOME is created when a manual install never did. Inverting the order inside the helper fails all three.

Worth noting the compass branch got the same treatment, so it no longer sweeps and then separately mkdirs — one shape on both paths.

727 green, lint clean.

Retracting my earlier approval — a deeper review found two correctness regressions introduced by moving the scratch into `IX_HOME`, one of which is data loss.

## Blocking: a failed download can delete the user's only working compass

`cleanupCompassSwap:615` tests `existsSync(join(compassDir, "index.html"))` and its comment is explicit about why: a `compass/` holding only a `.version` is a real state, and a bare `existsSync` "would call that 'back in place' and drop a backup the caller had just told the user to go and rescue."

`recover()` inside `sweepUpgradeOrphans` uses exactly that bare `existsSync(dest)`. So with `compass/` left as a `.version`-only husk and `.compass-backup-1234` holding the only real bundle, `recover()` declines to restore, and the loop below then deletes the backup.

On `main` that sweep ran *after* a successful download, so an offline run exited before reaching it and the backup survived for the next attempt. Hoisting the sweep above `curl` means **a run that installs nothing now destroys it** — the user sees only "[error] Failed to download", and `ix view` is permanently blank with no copy left on disk.

The two tests can't see this because they never construct the husk. Aligning `recover`'s test with `cleanupCompassSwap`'s (`index.html`, not bare `existsSync`) fixes it and makes the two agree.

## Blocking: concurrent `ix upgrade` deletes an in-flight download

The scratch moved from `os.tmpdir()`, where no sweep could match it, into `IX_HOME` with a swept prefix. Process A creates `.cli-download-AAAAAA` and starts a curl with a 300s timeout; process B — a second terminal, or `bootstrap.sh` re-running `ix upgrade` when it finds compass missing — calls `prepareDownloadDir` and deletes A's directory wholesale. On Linux/macOS curl's fd stays valid so A exits 0, then `tar -xzf` hits a missing path and A reports "Failed to extract CLI update" on a good download.

`.cli-staging-<pid>` has the same shape on main, but its window is the few seconds of extraction; this one is the whole download. Some ownership marker (pid in the name, skipped when that pid is live) would close both.

## Worth addressing

- `prepareDownloadDir` in the compass branch is the first filesystem write under `IX_HOME` and sits *outside* the try/catch that deliberately keeps compass failures non-fatal. On an unwritable `~/.ix` this turns "[!!] Compass extract failed / ix view keeps working" into a hard abort that also skips `writeCache`.
- Two bare `rmSync` calls (959, 1264) skip the retry treatment `rmQuiet` exists for — and this PR moves those directories into the user profile, where AV and indexer handles are the norm, which is precisely the case `rmQuiet`'s comment describes.

## One question before this lands

#349's reporter is on `C:\Users\Win 10` and their confirmed workaround was pointing TEMP at a space-free path. This moves the scratch from `C:\Users\WIN10~1\AppData\Local\Temp\...` (no space — 8.3 aliases never contain one) to `C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\.cli-download-...` (space). If the failure is space-driven rather than short-path-driven, the upgrade path now has the space where it previously didn't. "Refs #349" rather than "Fixes" is the right call, and the PR is honest that it's unreproduced — but "fixes the failure under every reading of it" doesn't hold under the space reading. Nothing in the suite sets `IX_HOME` to a path with a space.

Taking the upgrade path off TEMP is still right, and the `-download-` vs `-backup-` prefix reasoning is correct. It's the sweep's new reach that needs bounding.

Addressed in 5432c49 and b4d9c00, and rebased onto main now that #391 has landed.

**The data-loss path.** `recover()` now takes the file that proves the thing is real — `index.html` for the compass, `cli/dist/cli/main.js` for the install — so it applies the same test `cleanupCompassSwap` already applies. The two no longer disagree about a husk, so a torn swap restores the backup instead of the sweep deleting it. Verified: reverting to the bare `existsSync` fails two of the new cases.

**The concurrency window.** Download directories carry their pid (`.cli-download-<pid>-<rand>`) and the sweep skips one whose process is still addressable — `process.kill(pid, 0)`, treating EPERM as live. Unparseable names are treated as dead so the pre-pid naming stays collectable, and the guard is scoped to download prefixes so staging/backup reclaim behaviour is untouched. Verified: removing the guard fails the live-process case.

**The two bare `rmSync` calls** are now `rmQuiet`, which is the whole reason that helper exists — and this PR is what moves those directories from TEMP into the user profile.

**One more, found while composing the two PRs** (b4d9c00): both sweep calls sit behind "something needs updating", and #391 tightened the compass gate to skip release-bundled compasses — which is every install from v0.9.3 on. So on a healthy current install neither would fire and nothing would ever be reclaimed, which defeats the reason for sweeping the downloads at all. There is now one unconditional sweep at the top of a real `ix upgrade`; the calls inside `prepareDownloadDir` stay, since that is where the ordering invariant lives.

753 green on the rebased result, lint clean.

**Still open, and deliberately not resolved here:** whether #349 is space-driven or short-path-driven. The scratch now sits under `C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\...`, which contains the space, where the TEMP path it replaces did not. `Refs #349` is the right framing until someone reproduces it — worth keeping the issue open rather than closing it on this.

snapshot.title: feat(view): real /__ix/remap endpoint with loopback guard; fix WSL bootstrap
snapshot.body:
## Summary

Replaces the no-op `/__ix/remap` stub with a real endpoint that rebuilds the
code map by running `ix map .` in the visualizer's working directory. The
endpoint is hardened against CSRF and DNS-rebinding attacks and is only
accessible from loopback. Also fixes the WSL bootstrap to route through the
`curl|sh` installer path instead of the Windows PowerShell path.

## Motivation

The visualizer previously had no way to trigger a remap from the browser UI.
Users had to drop to a terminal and run `ix map .` manually. The `/__ix/remap`
route existed but was a stub that fell through to the SPA handler (returning
`index.html` with a 200, indistinguishable from any other unknown route).

## Files Changed

| File | Delta | Purpose |
|------|-------|---------|
| `ix-cli/src/cli/commands/view.ts` | +58/−3 | Real remap endpoint, loopback guard, client-disconnect child reaping, exported `serverScript` for testing |
| `ix-cli/test/view-server.test.ts` | +178 (new) | Full guard matrix tests (10 tests) |
| `skills/ix/scripts/bootstrap.sh` | +4/−5 | WSL installer fix, dead `node_ok` removal |
| `docs/api/README.md` | +13/−3 | Document the real endpoint and its security model |

**Total:** 4 files, +251/−10 lines

## Implementation

### Real `/__ix/remap` Endpoint

- `POST /__ix/remap` spawns `node <cli-main> map .` with a 30-minute timeout
- Responds `{ "ok": true }` on success, `{ "ok": false, "error": "..." }` on failure
- The map runs in `process.cwd()` — the workspace the visualizer was launched from

### Loopback-Only Security Model

The endpoint shells out with the user's full privileges, so it is guarded by a
double loopback check:

1. **Host check** — rejects requests where `Host` header is not `localhost`,
   `127.0.0.1`, or `[::1]`
2. **Origin check** — rejects cross-site `Origin` headers (any non-loopback
   hostname), malformed origins (URL parse failure), and non-http/https
   protocols; accepts missing `Origin` (curl-style, same-origin fetch)

Both must pass for the request to proceed. Failure returns `403
{ "ok": false, "error": "forbidden: loopback only" }`.

### Design Decisions

- **Origin parsed with `new URL()`**, not a regex: the server code lives inside
  a template literal in `serverScript()`. Regex backslashes would be consumed
  every time the server is regenerated by `ix view start`. The URL API avoids
  this class of bug entirely.
- **IPv6 bracketed literals**: `[::1]:8080` is correctly parsed by stripping
  the port from the closing bracket position, not by splitting on `:`.
- **Response "close" for client-disconnect reaping**: `res.on("close", ...)`
  with a `writableEnded` check distinguishes normal completion from abnormal
  client disconnect, avoiding killing the map mid-flight on certain Node
  versions that fire request `close` on completion.
- **`IX_VIEW_MAP_MAIN`**: test seam to point the server at a stub CLI instead
  of the real installation, enabling integration tests without a full build.

### Server Binding

The generated server binds explicitly to `127.0.0.1` (was previously `PORT`
only, which defaults to `::` on some Node versions).

### WSL Bootstrap Fix

`is_windows()` previously treated `WSL_DISTRO_NAME` as Windows, causing WSL
installs to take the PowerShell path. WSL is Linux (uname = Linux) and must
use the `curl|sh` path. Fixed by removing the WSL test from `is_windows()`.

## Security Model

### Guard Matrix

| Scenario | Origin | Host | Result |
|----------|--------|------|--------|
| Cross-site CSRF | `https://evil.example` | `127.0.0.1:PORT` | **403** |
| DNS rebinding | (any) | `attacker.example` | **403** |
| Malformed Origin | `not a url` | `127.0.0.1:PORT` | **403** |
| Non-loopback Origin | `http://10.0.0.5:8080` | `127.0.0.1:PORT` | **403** |
| Curl / no Origin | (absent) | `127.0.0.1:PORT` | **200** ✓ |
| Same-origin loopback | `http://localhost:PORT` | `127.0.0.1:PORT` | **200** ✓ |
| IPv6 loopback Host | (absent) | `[::1]:PORT` | **200** ✓ |
| GET (not POST) | — | — | SPA fallback (200, index.html) |

### What Is NOT Changed

- The server remains bound to `127.0.0.1` — never `0.0.0.0`
- The existing `/v1/*` proxy is untouched
- The SPA fallback behavior is preserved
- Existing view behavior (`ix view`) is unchanged
- No new dependencies added

## Tests

### New: `ix-cli/test/view-server.test.ts`

10 tests covering the complete guard matrix plus regression:

1. **cross-site CSRF** → 403 with correct error body
2. **DNS-rebinding Host** → 403 (uses raw `http.request` to bypass undici's Host protection)
3. **malformed Origin** → 403
4. **non-loopback Origin with loopback Host** → 403
5. **bracketed IPv6 Host** → 200
6. **no-Origin (curl-style)** → 200, map command runs (side-effect file verified)
7. **same-origin loopback Origin** → 200
8. **map command failure** → 500 with error string
9. **SPA fallback for GET /** → 200, returns index.html
10. **GET /__ix/remap** → SPA fallback (not treated as endpoint)

### Test Infrastructure

- Real server, real process spawn — no mocks for the server or child process
- Stub CLI (`IX_VIEW_MAP_MAIN`) controllable via `STUB_EXIT` env
- Template-literal integrity verified

## Verification Results

| Check | Result |
|-------|--------|
| Vitest (rebase base `ffe21f0`, 2026-08-11) | **730 passed, 2 skipped (732)** — includes the 10 guard tests |
| Merge-tree vs `ffe21f0` | exit 0, tree `de647175`, 0 conflicts |
| Patch equivalence | identical patch-id across rebases (`310dd4ab`) |
| Diff vs upstream | exactly 4 files, +251/−10 |
| TypeScript `--noEmit` | 0 errors |
| Working tree | Clean |

## Compatibility

- **Node**: No new minimum version requirement
- **Dependencies**: No new dependencies
- **API**: No breaking changes; `/__ix/remap` was a stub that returned SPA HTML
- **Config**: No new configuration
- **OS**: Loopback binding works on all platforms; WSL fix improves WSL compatibility

## Known Limitations

1. The remap endpoint has no rate limiting beyond the one-at-a-time constraint
   from the single-threaded server and client-disconnect reaping. This is
   acceptable for a loopback-only endpoint that the user controls.
2. The map command timeout (30 minutes) is generous. Very large workspaces
   could approach this limit.
3. The endpoint does not stream progress — the client waits for completion or
   timeout.

## Reviewer Notes

- The `serverScript` function is exported for testing. If adding more inline
  server logic, consider extracting to a separate file.
- The `res.on("close", ...)` with `writableEnded` guard handles a Node.js
  behavior difference: in some versions, the `IncomingMessage` (request)
  `close` event fires on normal completion, which would kill the map
  mid-flight. Using the `ServerResponse` (response) `close` event with the
  `writableEnded` check avoids this.

## Cross-References

- Issue #377 (remap stale symbols) — now closed upstream; this PR provides the
  browser-triggered remap capability.
- F-010/F-011/F-012 findings in the Ix-findings investigation.
- Separate from #390 (patches registration) and #391 (compass version series).

feat(view): real /__ix/remap endpoint with loopback guard; fix WSL bootstrap

Implements the reviewer-suggested follow-up (#368) in the source layer:

- view.ts serverScript now emits a real POST /__ix/remap handler that
  rebuilds the code map for the workspace the visualizer was launched from
  (its cwd) via the shipped CLI, instead of falling through to the SPA
  stub. The server binds 127.0.0.1, and the handler rejects non-loopback
  Hosts and non-loopback browser Origins (403), blocking CSRF and

  lives inside a template literal that is re-emitted on every ix view start.
  The CLI path is overridable via IX_VIEW_MAP_MAIN for tests, and the map
  child is reaped when the client disconnects before the response.
- bootstrap.sh: is_windows no longer treats WSL as Windows (uname is Linux
  there; it was being routed to the PowerShell installer), and the dead
  node_ok variable is removed.
- docs/api/README.md documents the real endpoint and its guard.

Verified: 656 vitest tests pass (10 new view-server tests covering the
guard matrix, success/failure, SPA fallback, loopback bind), tsc clean,
eslint clean.

  client disconnect, avoiding killing the map mid-flight on certain Node
  versions that fire request `close` on completion.
- **`IX_VIEW_MAP_MAIN`**: test seam to point the server at a stub CLI instead
  of the real installation, enabling integration tests without a full build.

### Server Binding

The generated server binds explicitly to `127.0.0.1` (was previously `PORT`
only, which defaults to `::` on some Node versions).

### WSL Bootstrap Fix

`is_windows()` previously treated `WSL_DISTRO_NAME` as Windows, causing WSL
installs to take the PowerShell path. WSL is Linux (uname = Linux) and must
use the `curl|sh` path. Fixed by removing the WSL test from `is_windows()`.

## Security Model

### Guard Matrix

| Scenario | Origin | Host | Result |
|----------|--------|------|--------|
| Cross-site CSRF | `https://evil.example` | `127.0.0.1:PORT` | **403** |
| DNS rebinding | (any) | `attacker.example` | **403** |
| Malformed Origin | `not a url` | `127.0.0.1:PORT` | **403** |
| Non-loopback Origin | `http://10.0.0.5:8080` | `127.0.0.1:PORT` | **403** |
| Curl / no Origin | (absent) | `127.0.0.1:PORT` | **200** ✓ |
| Same-origin loopback | `http://localhost:PORT` | `127.0.0.1:PORT` | **200** ✓ |
| IPv6 loopback Host | (absent) | `[::1]:PORT` | **200** ✓ |
| GET (not POST) | — | — | SPA fallback (200, index.html) |

### What Is NOT Changed

- The server remains bound to `127.0.0.1` — never `0.0.0.0`
- The existing `/v1/*` proxy is untouched
- The SPA fallback behavior is preserved
- Existing view behavior (`ix view`) is unchanged
- No new dependencies added

## Tests

### New: `ix-cli/test/view-server.test.ts`

10 tests covering the complete guard matrix plus regression:

1. **cross-site CSRF** → 403 with correct error body
2. **DNS-rebinding Host** → 403 (uses raw `http.request` to bypass undici's Host protection)
3. **malformed Origin** → 403
4. **non-loopback Origin with loopback Host** → 403
5. **bracketed IPv6 Host** → 200
6. **no-Origin (curl-style)** → 200, map command runs (side-effect file verified)
7. **same-origin loopback Origin** → 200
8. **map command failure** → 500 with error string
9. **SPA fallback for GET /** → 200, returns index.html
10. **GET /__ix/remap** → SPA fallback (not treated as endpoint)

### Test Infrastructure

- Real server, real process spawn — no mocks for the server or child process
- Stub CLI (`IX_VIEW_MAP_MAIN`) controllable via `STUB_EXIT` env
- Template-literal integrity verified

## Verification Results

| Check | Result |
|-------|--------|
| Vitest (rebase base `ffe21f0`, 2026-08-11) | **730 passed, 2 skipped (732)** — includes the 10 guard tests |
| Merge-tree vs `ffe21f0` | exit 0, tree `de647175`, 0 conflicts |
| Patch equivalence | identical patch-id across rebases (`310dd4ab`) |
| Diff vs upstream | exactly 4 files, +251/−10 |
| TypeScript `--noEmit` | 0 errors |
| Working tree | Clean |

## Compatibility

- **Node**: No new minimum version requirement
- **Dependencies**: No new dependencies
- **API**: No breaking changes; `/__ix/remap` was a stub that returned SPA HTML
- **Config**: No new configuration
- **OS**: Loopback binding works on all platforms; WSL fix improves WSL compatibility

## Known Limitations

1. The remap endpoint has no rate limiting beyond the one-at-a-time constraint
   from the single-threaded server and client-disconnect reaping. This is
   acceptable for a loopback-only endpoint that the user controls.
2. The map command timeout (30 minutes) is generous. Very large workspaces
   could approach this limit.
3. The endpoint does not stream progress — the client waits for completion or
   timeout.

## Reviewer Notes

- The `serverScript` function is exported for testing. If adding more inline
  server logic, consider extracting to a separate file.
- The `res.on("close", ...)` with `writableEnded` guard handles a Node.js
  behavior difference: in some versions, the `IncomingMessage` (request)
  `close` event fires on normal completion, which would kill the map
  mid-flight. Using the `ServerResponse` (response) `close` event with the
  `writableEnded` check avoids this.

## Cross-References

- Issue #377 (remap stale symbols) — now closed upstream; this PR provides the
  browser-triggered remap capability.
- F-010/F-011/F-012 findings in the Ix-findings investigation.
- Separate from #390 (patches registration) and #391 (compass version series).

feat(view): real /__ix/remap endpoint with loopback guard; fix WSL bootstrap

Implements the reviewer-suggested follow-up (#368) in the source layer:

- view.ts serverScript now emits a real POST /__ix/remap handler that
  rebuilds the code map for the workspace the visualizer was launched from
  (its cwd) via the shipped CLI, instead of falling through to the SPA
  stub. The server binds 127.0.0.1, and the handler rejects non-loopback
  Hosts and non-loopback browser Origins (403), blocking CSRF and
  DNS-rebinding on an endpoint that shells out with the user's privileges.
  The Origin is parsed with the URL API (not a regex) because the snippet
  lives inside a template literal that is re-emitted on every ix view start.
  The CLI path is overridable via IX_VIEW_MAP_MAIN for tests, and the map
  child is reaped when the client disconnects before the response.
- bootstrap.sh: is_windows no longer treats WSL as Windows (uname is Linux
  there; it was being routed to the PowerShell installer), and the dead
  node_ok variable is removed.
- docs/api/README.md documents the real endpoint and its guard.

Verified: 656 vitest tests pass (10 new view-server tests covering the
guard matrix, success/failure, SPA fallback, loopback bind), tsc clean,
eslint clean.

fix(view): scope the remap to the workspace, and serialise it

Follow-up to the review of this PR. The guard itself held against every
probe I could think of — Origin: null, file://, data:, userinfo tricks,
trailing-dot Host, short-form IPv4, absolute-form request lines, path
traversal, percent-encoding — so what follows is about what happens
*after* a request is allowed through.

**The remap mapped the server's cwd.** `ix view start` spawns the
detached server with no cwd option, so it inherits wherever it was
launched, and remap ran `ix map .` there. `--all` deliberately does not
require the cwd to be a workspace (view.ts opts out of resolveWorkspaceId
entirely), and CLAUDE.md documents `ix view start --all --no-open` as the
normal invocation — so starting it from a home directory turned one click
into an ingest of the whole of it. The workspace root is now resolved by
`ix view start`, by the same lookup that produces the x-ix-workspace
header, and baked into the script; an unscoped view answers 409 instead
of falling back to the cwd.

That reach was not limited to the button. The Origin check accepted any
loopback hostname on any port, and a simple POST needs no preflight, so
any page served on another localhost port could trigger it. Origin must
now match this server's port too.

**Nothing serialised the maps.** execFile is asynchronous: 12 concurrent
POSTs started 12 concurrent `ix map` runs over the same workspace,
measured. The client's in-flight flag is per-tab, so two tabs were enough.
One at a time now, 409 while busy.

**MAP_MAIN is baked in rather than re-derived.** `resolve(DIST, "..",
"..")` only yields IX_HOME for the installed layout; findCompassDist's
dev branch returns a repo path, from which the same arithmetic lands on a
file that never exists. It now comes from this module's own location at
generation time, which holds for both. The IX_VIEW_MAP_MAIN seam is
honoured only under NODE_ENV=test, so a shipped install cannot be
redirected to an arbitrary script through the environment.

`--silent` and an explicit maxBuffer: nothing reads that stdout, and the
default 1 MiB makes Node SIGTERM the child mid-map, surfacing as a 500
rather than as the truncation it is. Reachable only if the output ever
grows with the repo — today the tree render is capped at --max-items and
ingest prints a fixed summary — but the map does not need to render at
all. The request body is drained rather than left open for the map's
duration.

Two in bootstrap.sh, both pre-existing:

- The backticks in the docker warning were command substitutions, not
  quoting. The failure path re-ran `ix docker start`, then ran `ix doctor`
  and `ix status`, spliced their stdout into the message, and left the
  user with the command names stripped out of the advice.
- is_windows() had dropped MSYSTEM along with WSL_DISTRO_NAME, which the
  comment justified only for WSL. Restored; the WSL fix is untouched.

Tests move to src/cli/__tests__/ — tsconfig is include: ["src"], so at
their old path CI never type-checked them. They no longer leak a temp
directory per run or write a marker into the package root, and replacing
the server now awaits the old child's exit rather than re-binding the
port under it. 10 -> 13 tests; the three new ones each fail against a
mutant of the guard they cover.

735 tests pass; typecheck, lint and knip clean.

snapshot.title: test(upgrade): cover an IX_HOME containing a space
snapshot.body:
Closes the one open question from the #391/#392 review. Everything else Joey raised is fixed and merged — I verified the two blocking ones independently before writing this:

- the stamp is now `0.9.4+release.<sha>`, and running it through `main`'s own `splitVersion`/`isNewer` gives `[0,9,4]`, `[1,0,0]`, `[2,3,1]` with **no downgrade at any version**;
- `recover()` now tests `existsSync(join(dest, intact))` rather than the bare directory, so a `.version`-only husk no longer counts as present and the backup survives.

## The question this covers

#349's reporter is on `C:\Users\Win 10`, and their confirmed workaround was pointing TEMP at a space-free path.

#392 moved the upgrade scratch from `C:\Users\WIN10~1\AppData\Local\Temp\...` — an 8.3 alias, which **never contains a space** — to `C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\...`, which does. If that failure is space-driven rather than short-path-driven, the move put a space onto the upgrade path where there previously wasn't one.

## What this can and cannot do

It **cannot settle the mechanism.** It runs on whatever platform CI is on, and the suspected fault is a Windows path provider.

What it does is prove our own code carries no space-free assumption — so when the reporter tries again, the remaining suspects are outside this repo. Nothing else in the suite passed a path with a space.

Four cases: preparing a download directory inside a spaced `IX_HOME`, creating one a manual install never made, sweeping orphans out of it, and restoring an interrupted install into it.

## One thing worth reporting from writing it

The sweep case first used `.cli-download-1-abc` and **failed** — pid 1 is init, always alive, so the sweep correctly skipped the directory as an in-flight download owned by another process. That is `isLiveScratch` doing exactly its job, on the first real attempt to trip it. The test now uses a pid that is not running.

759 tests green · tsc clean · lint unchanged (0 errors, 38 pre-existing warnings).

snapshot.title: fix(config): respect workspace path boundaries
snapshot.body:
Fixes #402

## Summary

Prevent workspace lookup from treating an unrelated sibling directory whose name shares a prefix as part of a registered workspace.

## Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Test
- [ ] CI

## Changes

- Match workspace roots using path-component boundaries instead of raw string prefixes.
- Preserve nearest-workspace selection for nested workspaces.
- Add regression coverage for exact roots, descendants, sibling prefixes, and nested roots.

## Validation

- `npm test` (61 files, 843 tests, including parser smoke tests)
- `npm run typecheck`
- `npm run build`
- Targeted ESLint and Prettier checks
- Live synthetic reproduction with a distinct default workspace. A sibling path no longer resolves a symbol mapped only from the prefix-sharing workspace.

## Checklist

- [x] Tests pass
- [x] Smoke tests pass
- [x] No raw errors introduced
- [x] CLI output follows Ix format

## Release checklist (if merging to main)

- [ ] `ix-cli/package.json` version bumped
- [ ] After merge: tag pushed (`git tag vX.Y.Z && git push origin vX.Y.Z`)
- [ ] If backend changes: `ix-memory-layer` tagged and released first
- [ ] If `docker-compose.standalone.yml` changed: verified `curl | sh` install works

snapshot.body:
An independent review of #400 found that three of its own fixes were wrong, and that two of its tests were written so they could not fail against the defect they claimed to cover. All were reproduced before fixing.

## Three fixes in #400 were wrong

**An orphan settling mid-run released the *running* command's lock.** `releaseHeldLocks` drops every lock the process holds, not the finishing command's — and the guard only asked whether an orphan was in flight, never whether something was running right now. A command abandoned at its timeout, settling part-way through an unrelated `ix map`, deleted that map's lock and reopened the exact window single-flight exists to close. The guard now also requires `activeRun === null`, which the lock-holding command's own `finally` always satisfies, so nothing is stranded.

**A command that never settles was an immortal orphan.** `finished` derives from `work`; if `work` never settles, the entry could never be removed. Everything keyed off it then failed permanently open, for the life of the server:

- `exitCodeIsOurs` stayed false, so **every** later failing command reported `ok: true` — the precise inverse of the misclassification #400 set out to fix.
- `releaseHeldLocks()` never ran again, so the second `ix_map` coalesced — the headline bug of #400, restored.

Membership is now bounded by a grace timer as well as by the command settling. `installServerErrorHandlers` made non-settling commands *more likely*, since an exception that used to end the process is now only logged, which is what made this reachable.

**Staleness by regex both missed and misfired.** `[^"'\s,\]]*` cannot cross a space, so `C:\Users\Jane Doe\...\ix.cmd` — the common Windows shape, not the edge one — went on reading as healthy. And allowing a match to start at an interior `/` made it latch onto the `/npm/ix.cmd` suffix of a *live* path, report it stale, and silently rewrite a working registration with no `--force` (plus `doctor` exiting 1 on a healthy machine). The launcher is now read from the parsed entry, so there is nothing to guess; an unreachable path is still not "gone", since only ENOENT counts.

## A quoting hole, and two tests that could not fail

**`quoteForCmd` passed cmd metacharacters through bare.** Its fast path tested only whitespace and quotes, so a path with `&`, `^` or `|` and no space was emitted unquoted. Verified by round-trip against a real `cmd` invocation:

| argument | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `C:\Users\R&D\npm\ix.cmd` | arrives as `C:\Users\R`; cmd runs `D\npm\ix.cmd` as a second command | intact |
| `C:\a^b\ix.cmd` | arrives silently as `C:\ab\ix.cmd`, `ok: true` | intact |
| `C:\a\|b\ix.cmd` | mangled | intact |

The reachable input is `resolveLauncher()`'s output — the user's own npm prefix path. The predicate is now a whitelist, and `%` joins `"` as unencodable rather than being expanded by cmd behind the quoting's back.

**The two tests that could not fail are replaced.** The `quoteForCmd` fixture contained a space, so it took the quoting branch either way and never exercised the bare path; the stale-launcher fixture used the one path shape the broken regex happened to match. Both now cover the defect.

## Also

- `MISSING_ENTRY` is tied to our own server name, so an unrelated "not found" in a host's output can no longer read as a free name and overwrite the user's server.
- OpenClaw's Windows write is paired with a matching Windows read, so the platform that writes the file also reads it — the asymmetry VS Code was explicitly fixed for.
- The README no longer claims a write path Windows does not take.
- Tests that reach `acquireMapLock` no longer write into the developer's real `~/.ix/locks`.

## Verification

- `typecheck` clean, lint unchanged from baseline (0 errors, same 41 warnings), knip clean.
- 76 tests pass across the three `mcp` suites.
- **All five fixes validated by restoring the defect** and confirming the intended test — not merely the suite — goes red. One of them caught a sixth test that had silently failed to apply and was not in the file at all.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

test(mcp): scope the UNC staleness case to Windows

A UNC path is a network location only on Windows, where stat fails on an
unreachable one with something other than ENOENT — which is the whole point of
the assertion. Everywhere else those backslashes are ordinary filename
characters, the path really is absent, and `stale` is the right answer, so the
test failed on both Linux runners and both macOS runners while passing on
Windows where it was written. Confirmed against Linux directly rather than by
another CI round-trip.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(mcp): stop the grace path releasing a live lock, restore listing staleness

A review of the previous commit found two regressions in it.

**The grace timer released the lock of a command that was still running.**
`forget()` dropped orphan-set membership *and* ran `afterCommand`. On the settle
path that is right; on the grace path the command is by definition still
working, so `releaseHeldLocks()` deleted the single-flight lock of a map still
in progress — a second `ix map` could then take the workspace out from under it,
which is the window single-flight exists to close. `ix_map` gets 120s, so its
grace is 120s: a map overrunning by that much lost its lock mid-run. The same
call reset the read scope mid-ingest, and because the settle path then
short-circuited, it never reset again — leaving the pre-map scope pinned with
nothing left to invalidate it. The grace now only drops membership; settle
always runs `afterCommand`.

**Staleness detection had gone dead for Claude Code, Codex and Gemini.**
Reading the launcher only from a parsed entry left the three hosts that answer
with a rendered table — and the three that record an absolute `ix.cmd` on
Windows — with no launcher at all, so `judge` skipped the check entirely. After
an nvm switch or a moved npm prefix those hosts read as healthy again and
`install` skipped the repair: the exact failure `stale` was added to fix,
restored where it mattered most, and invisible to a suite whose install/doctor
tests inject the registration directly.

The listing row is read again, but anchored to a token boundary and with a lazy
body: the anchor is what stops a match beginning at an interior `/` and latching
onto the `/npm/ix.cmd` suffix of a live path, and the lazy body is what lets it
span `C:\Users\Jane Doe\...`. Both faults the first regex had, without giving up
the coverage. Tests now use the real `claude`/`codex`/`gemini` listing shapes,
and the false-positive fixture uses a path that exists, contains a space and
uses forward slashes — without all three it cannot tell the behaviours apart.

Also from the review: openclaw's Windows read goes back through
`openclaw mcp show`, which cmd handles fine and which is the only check that the
shape written there is one openclaw actually reads — pairing it with the file
write traded a loud `not registered` for a silent `already registered`. The
comment on the grace bound now says plainly that its cost lands on a later call
rather than on the abandoned command. And the README no longer implies OpenClaw
is detected by a config directory; it is still detected on PATH.

Validated by restoring each defect and confirming the intended test goes red,
and the timing-sensitive runner suite was run five times over to check it is
not flaky.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(mcp): scope lock release to the command that took the lock

A third review found the previous commit only deferred the lock bug by one tool
call, and introduced a regression of its own.

**Deferred, not fixed.** Removing `afterCommand` from the grace path left the
release guard reading `liveOrphans.size === 0` — and the grace deliberately
removes a still-running command from that set. So the next command to complete
released the abandoned one's lock anyway, mid-run. The set was doing two jobs
with different lifetimes: "this command's exit code is untrustworthy", which
must be bounded, and "this command is still running", which must not be.

Locks are now owned. `single-flight` records which command took each lock and
releases only that command's, so the question stops being global: a command that
overran its timeout keeps the lock it is still using, and a different command
that has genuinely finished still gives its own up. Both directions were broken
before — releasing everything took a running map's lock, and holding everything
back to avoid that stranded a finished map's.

**Regression.** Moving `resetReadScope` to the settle handler alone meant a
command that never settles — the case the grace exists for — never invalidated
at all. It runs on the grace as well now; it is idempotent, so covering both
costs nothing.

**`launcherInText`, third attempt.** Reading the row left to right was the flaw
common to both previous versions: the match began at the first absolute-looking
token and ran forward, so `cmd /c C:\...\ix.cmd` — the documented Windows
wrapper form — yielded `/c C:\...\ix.cmd` and reported a live launcher dead,
which re-registers with no `--force`. It now anchors on the `ix` end and walks
back to the nearest absolute-path start, so a preceding flag or an earlier path
on the same row cannot be swallowed, and a launcher under `C:\Users\Jane Doe\`
is still found. Four wrapper shapes are pinned by tests.

Also: the orphan drain moved from `withLockDir` to a file-level `afterEach`.
Abandoned commands outlive the test that starts them and the runner's state is
module-level, so every later test saw distrusted exit codes and a held lock —
correct behaviour, silently changing unrelated assertions. Under
`--sequence.shuffle.tests` that failed 4 of 6 seeds; all 6 are clean now.

Each fix validated by restoring the defect and confirming the intended test goes
red, and the ownership one checked by mutating single-flight to ignore the owner.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(mcp): stop parsing the launcher out of a listing row

A fourth review found the previous commit reported `C:\Program Files (x86)\...`
as stale: trimming a row's punctuation was applied to every token, including
the interior tokens of a path that had just been split on its own spaces, so
the rejoin produced `C:\Program Files x86)\...` and stat'd nothing. Brackets
and commas in a username did the same. That is the most common path shape on
Windows, and `stale` re-registers with no `--force`, so it silently rewrote
working configs — the exact failure the rewrite existed to remove.

That is four attempts at recovering a path from a rendered table, each broken
on a different shape: stopping at the first space missed `C:\Users\Jane Doe`;
scanning forward swallowed a `cmd /c` prefix; walking back from the `ix` anchor
fell to delimiter trimming. The approach is the defect. Table rows are
space-delimited and paths contain spaces; there is no parse that is right.

So it stops parsing. Staleness only ever needed to establish whether the row
records the launcher we would write today, and a row that does contains that
string verbatim, whatever surrounds it. Containment, case-insensitive with
separators normalised. No tokens, no delimiters, no reconstruction — and no
path shape left to get wrong. The parsed-entry path is unchanged, since a
recorded command needs no guessing at all. `resolveLauncher` is memoised
because `doctor` now consults it once per host.

Tests cover every host row format against every launcher shape that has broken
an attempt — spaces, `(x86)`, brackets, a comma, a wrapper prefix, quotes — in
both directions, which the previous one-directional set did not.

Also from the review: the lock-owner resolver no longer falls back to
`activeRun`. For output that fallback only narrows the damage, but an owner
guessed wrong for a lock means a *different* command's settle deletes a lock
still in use; unattributed is the safe direction. Two comments describing
mechanisms this PR removed are corrected, and the test drain drops from 500ms
to 250 — it was costing ~11s on one file for no coverage.

Every fix validated by restoring the defect, including reinstating the whole
parsing approach to confirm the `(x86)` case goes red. 8/8 shuffle seeds clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(mcp): drop launcher staleness for the CLI-listed hosts, and make --force work

A fifth review found the containment check regressed the case it was meant to
protect, and that the repair it feeds could not land on the flagship host
anyway. Both were demonstrated against the real `claude` and `codex` binaries.

**The regression.** `run()` decodes host output as UTF-8, but a Windows console
emits the OEM code page, so `where ix` returns a non-ASCII npm prefix mangled.
The row holds the real path and `expected` holds the mangled one, so a working
registration read as stale — and `install` then overwrote a config the user had
repaired by hand with a launcher that cannot start, no `--force` required. That
is the failure the previous commit said it existed to remove, reached by a
different road.

**The repair could not land.** `claude mcp add` refuses a name that already
exists and has no force flag. Seeding an isolated Claude config and running the
real `runInstall` gave `outcome: failed`, note `"MCP server ix-memory already
exists in user config"`, config unchanged — for a stale entry *and* for a
foreign one under `--force`. So `--force` was inert for Claude Code, which the
README advertises.

Staleness from a rendered listing row is therefore gone rather than fixed
again. Five attempts, five variants of the same failure: a working registration
called stale, which re-registers without `--force`. A moved npm prefix on
Claude Code, Codex and Gemini is now a manual `ix mcp install --force`. That is
a real gap, and a smaller one than silently rewriting configs that were fine.
Hosts whose config we read directly keep it: there the recorded command is
exact, and the repair is a file write that works.

`--force` is fixed independently, since it was broken for conflicts too:
`register` now takes whether it is replacing something, and hosts whose `add`
will not overwrite clear the name first. Verified against the real `claude`
binary — a foreign registration under `--force` now yields `registered` with
the entry replaced, where before it was `failed` with the entry untouched.

The launcher-shape test matrix goes with the feature it covered; the removal
argv is pinned instead, because the wiring is only observable against a host
binary CI does not have.

Six mutations caught by the intended test, 10/10 shuffle seeds clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fell to delimiter trimming. The approach is the defect. Table rows are
space-delimited and paths contain spaces; there is no parse that is right.

So it stops parsing. Staleness only ever needed to establish whether the row
records the launcher we would write today, and a row that does contains that
string verbatim, whatever surrounds it. Containment, case-insensitive with
separators normalised. No tokens, no delimiters, no reconstruction — and no
path shape left to get wrong. The parsed-entry path is unchanged, since a
recorded command needs no guessing at all. `resolveLauncher` is memoised
because `doctor` now consults it once per host.

Tests cover every host row format against every launcher shape that has broken
an attempt — spaces, `(x86)`, brackets, a comma, a wrapper prefix, quotes — in
both directions, which the previous one-directional set did not.

Also from the review: the lock-owner resolver no longer falls back to
`activeRun`. For output that fallback only narrows the damage, but an owner
guessed wrong for a lock means a *different* command's settle deletes a lock
still in use; unattributed is the safe direction. Two comments describing
mechanisms this PR removed are corrected, and the test drain drops from 500ms
to 250 — it was costing ~11s on one file for no coverage.

Every fix validated by restoring the defect, including reinstating the whole
parsing approach to confirm the `(x86)` case goes red. 8/8 shuffle seeds clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(mcp): drop launcher staleness for the CLI-listed hosts, and make --force work

A fifth review found the containment check regressed the case it was meant to
protect, and that the repair it feeds could not land on the flagship host
anyway. Both were demonstrated against the real `claude` and `codex` binaries.

**The regression.** `run()` decodes host output as UTF-8, but a Windows console
emits the OEM code page, so `where ix` returns a non-ASCII npm prefix mangled.
The row holds the real path and `expected` holds the mangled one, so a working
registration read as stale — and `install` then overwrote a config the user had
repaired by hand with a launcher that cannot start, no `--force` required. That
is the failure the previous commit said it existed to remove, reached by a
different road.

**The repair could not land.** `claude mcp add` refuses a name that already
exists and has no force flag. Seeding an isolated Claude config and running the
real `runInstall` gave `outcome: failed`, note `"MCP server ix-memory already
exists in user config"`, config unchanged — for a stale entry *and* for a
foreign one under `--force`. So `--force` was inert for Claude Code, which the
README advertises.

Staleness from a rendered listing row is therefore gone rather than fixed
again. Five attempts, five variants of the same failure: a working registration
called stale, which re-registers without `--force`. A moved npm prefix on
Claude Code, Codex and Gemini is now a manual `ix mcp install --force`. That is
a real gap, and a smaller one than silently rewriting configs that were fine.
Hosts whose config we read directly keep it: there the recorded command is
exact, and the repair is a file write that works.

`--force` is fixed independently, since it was broken for conflicts too:
`register` now takes whether it is replacing something, and hosts whose `add`
will not overwrite clear the name first. Verified against the real `claude`
binary — a foreign registration under `--force` now yields `registered` with
the entry replaced, where before it was `failed` with the entry untouched.

The launcher-shape test matrix goes with the feature it covered; the removal
argv is pinned instead, because the wiring is only observable against a host
binary CI does not have.

Six mutations caught by the intended test, 10/10 shuffle seeds clean.
